title: Emerging Technologies and Data Analysis in Movement Disorder Assessments - Volume II
summary: Movement disorders encompass a broad range of neurological conditions characterized by hypokinetic, hyperkinetic states, or both. The abnormal expression of voluntary movement can be measured in the clinical setting using a variety of tools. There is increasing evidence that these technological advancements can enhance the accuracy of diagnosis and clinical decisions on treatments. Despite considerable progress, challenges remain in achieving early diagnosis, continuous monitoring, and personalized treatment strategies.

title: Innovative signal processing algorithms: Machine learning, deep learning, AI
summary: The human brain generates an extraordinary volume of complex, high-dimensional signals, from electroencephalographic (EEG) and magnetoencephalographic (MEG) recordings to functional MRI time series and intracranial local field potentials. Decoding these signals with sufficient precision to advance our understanding of neural function and to translate that understanding into clinical tools, represents one of the defining challenges of modern neuroscience. Conventional signal processing approaches, while foundational, are increasingly insufficient in the face of data complexity, inter-subject variability, and the subtlety of neural dynamics that underlie cognition, perception, and disease.
image_alt: Innovative signal processing algorithms: Machine learning, deep learning, AI

title: Non-invasive brain stimulation as a causal tool to map and modulate hippocampal–cortical circuits
summary: Recent research has shown that non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) in particular, can modulate core memory processes, including encoding, consolidation, and retrieval, across domains, such as episodic, spatial, associative, and working memory.
image_alt: Non-invasive brain stimulation as a causal tool to map and modulate hippocampal–cortical circuits

title: The Parkinsonian Spectrum: Dissecting Convergent Mechanisms
summary: The etiology of the progressive neurodegeneration that characterizes Parkinson’s disease (PD) remains relatively enigmatic, despite immense advances in our understanding of the condition. Pivotal elements that underpin current viewpoints include vital contributions from both molecular genetics and also from greatly improved understanding of the nature of aggregated proteins, which carry the potential to propagate throughout the nervous system.
image_alt: The Parkinsonian Spectrum: Dissecting Convergent Mechanisms

title: Enabling Sustainable Return-to-Work and Reintegration After Illness and Chronic Conditions
summary: Population aging represents one of the major challenges for occupational and healthcare systems in industrialized countries. The increase in retirement age, together with demographic changes and the progressive extension of working life, has led to a growing proportion of older workers within the labor market. At the same time, the rising average age of the workforce is associated with a higher prevalence of chronic diseases, multimorbidity, and health conditions that may result in prolonged sickness absence.

title: Motivational Functioning in Educational Settings: Psychological Processes, Beliefs, and Professional Well-Being
Neural basis of substance use and addiction: Recent findings and treatment implications
summary: Addiction remains one of the most pressing public health challenges of our time, and the landscape is shifting fast. The rise of synthetic opioids and polysubstance use, the explosion of behavioral and digital addictions (gaming, social media, gambling), and breakthrough treatments once considered fringe — such as GLP-1 receptor agonists and psychedelic-assisted therapies — have transformed both the questions we ask and the tools we use to answer them. At the same time, advances in human neuroscience, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence are giving us unprecedented resolution into the neural mechanisms that drive compulsive behavior and, crucially, recovery.

title: Next-gen neuro-AI: Aligning foundation models and biologically plausible architectures with human cognition
summary: Cognitive computational neuroscience has entered a transformative era. The rapid rise of large multimodal foundation models, state-space architectures, and advanced transformers has shifted the conversation: we are no longer just building artificial intelligence to solve tasks, but actively using these models as candidate mathematical "theories of the mind." By comparing the latent representations of artificial neural networks with biological neural activity, researchers are uncovering unprecedented insights into human perception, memory, decision-making, and language.

title: Sleep to Think: Multimodal Mechanisms Linking Sleep, Learning, and Performance
summary: Sleep is not merely a passive state but a dynamic process fundamental to learning, memory consolidation, and cognitive performance. During sleep, the brain undergoes remarkable transformations—reorganizing neural circuits, strengthening newly acquired memories, and clearing metabolic waste accumulated during wakefulness. Decades of research have established that adequate sleep enhances learning capacity, improves problem-solving, and optimizes performance across academic, athletic, and professional domains. Conversely, sleep deprivation impairs attention, working memory, and executive function. Yet the precise multimodal mechanisms linking sleep architecture, electrophysiological activity, neurochemical processes, and behavioral outcomes remain incompletely understood. Recent advances in polysomnography, neuroimaging, electrophysiology, computational modeling, and biomarker assessment have enabled more sophisticated investigation of sleep-dependent learning and performance. Understandi

title: Reimagining Human Movement: The Impact of Extended Reality on Physical and Emotional Experience, Volume II
summary: Extended Reality (XR), encompassing Virtual, Augmented, and Mixed Reality, has rapidly moved from novelty to a credible tool for shaping how humans learn, train, recover, and express movement. Volume I of this Research Topic attracted broad engagement across motor learning, neurorehabilitation, sport performance, and creative movement, confirming a vibrant interdisciplinary community working at the intersection of immersive technology and human physicality. It also exposed three areas where the evidence base remains thin: durable, long-term effects of XR-based movement training; applications across the full lifespan, in particular healthy aging and clinical populations; and inclusive, equitable design of immersive movement experiences. Volume II builds directly on this momentum, deepening the scientific conversation rather than restarting it, and broadening the contributor pool toward clinical, developmental, and applied settings.
image_alt: Reimagining Human Movement: The Impact of Extended Reality on Physical and Emotional Experience, Volume II

title: Brain–body interactions in neuropsychiatric and neurological disorders
summary: Understanding the complex communication between the brain and peripheral systems has become central to human neuroscience. Recent research highlights that the central nervous system interacts dynamically with the immune, endocrine, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal systems, influencing both brain function and behaviour across the lifespan. Dysregulation in these bidirectional networks is increasingly implicated in the development and progression of neuropsychiatric and neurological disorders such as depression, schizophrenia, Parkinson’s disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. Emerging evidence from neuroimaging, multi-omics, and clinical studies underscores the role of systemic inflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and gut–brain signalling in shaping cognitive and emotional processes. Despite these advances, a comprehensive understanding of how brain–body interactions contribute to the onset, progression, and treatment response of these disorders remains incomplete. Addressing this gap re
image_alt: Brain–body interactions in neuropsychiatric and neurological disorders

title: Multimodal data integration for precision brain health
summary: Breakthroughs in human neuroscience have enabled the generation of diverse and high-dimensional data from genomics and epigenomics, advanced neuroimaging, fluid and digital biomarkers, as well as cognitive and behavioral assessments. Despite these advances, single-modality studies often fall short in capturing the complexity of brain health and disease, leaving gaps in our understanding of nervous system development, mechanisms underlying neuropsychiatric and neurological conditions, and factors affecting brain aging. Recent research has demonstrated the potential of integrating data across multiple biological and behavioral domains to uncover novel biomarkers, patient subtypes, and mechanistic insights. However, challenges remain around analytic integration, clinical translation, and ensuring reproducibility and equity in findings.
image_alt: Multimodal data integration for precision brain health

title: Novel Molecular and Cellular Targets Driving Axon Regeneration After Spinal Cord Injury
summary: Spinal cord injury (SCI) leads to devastating and often irreversible loss of sensory and motor function due to the limited regenerative capacity of the adult central nervous system. Axon regeneration, the ability of injured neurons to re-extend functional projections, is a critical prerequisite for restoring connectivity and neurological recovery. Despite decades of research, the molecular and cellular mechanisms that govern axon regeneration remain only partially understood. This Research Topic aims to highlight emerging molecular and cellular targets that drive axon regeneration following spinal cord injury. By integrating discoveries from transcriptomic profiling, genetic manipulation, and advanced imaging, this collection seeks to uncover new regulatory pathways and therapeutic strategies that promote axonal growth and synaptic reconnection after injury.
image_alt: Novel Molecular and Cellular Targets Driving Axon Regeneration After Spinal Cord Injury

Pushed to Choose: Motivational, Emotional, and Physiological Processes in Police Decision-Making
summary: Police decision-making often unfolds in emotionally charged, uncertain, and time-pressured environments. Officers are required to interpret ambiguous cues, regulate affect, assess risk, and act in ways that are lawful, proportionate, and operationally effective. Yet these decisions are not shaped by cognition alone. Emotional states, chronic occupational stress, fatigue, burnout, trauma exposure, moral strain, and psychological well-being can all influence attention, judgment, impulse control, communication, and post-incident recovery. At the same time, the consequences of police decisions extend beyond individual performance to public trust, procedural justice, use-of-force outcomes, and officers’ long-term mental health. A focused discussion of how emotional processes and well-being interact with police decision-making is therefore timely and necessary, both for psychological theory and for evidence-informed practice.
image_alt: Pushed to Choose: Motivational, Emotional, and Physiological Processes in Police Decision-Making

title: Remodeling of blood-brain barrier function: implications for stroke therapy and clinical translation
summary: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), typically caused by hypertension or aneurysm rupture, is a devastating subtype of stroke. ICH accounts for approximately 15% of all stroke cases and is characterized by high mortality and morbidity. Despite advances in neurocritical care, clinical interventions such as hematoma evacuation rarely improve neurological outcomes. Studies have found that ICH causes not only primary brain injury but also secondary brain injury after hemorrhage, in which disruption of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is a central event, contributing to peri-hematomal edema, hematoma expansion, and ultimately neuronal damage. The neurovascular unit (NVU) is the core component of the BBB and is composed of endothelial cells, astrocytes, pericytes, neurons, and the extracellular matrix.

title: Translational brain imaging–guided neuromodulation
summary: The intersection of advanced neuroimaging and neuromodulation is reshaping how we understand and treat disorders of the nervous system. Techniques such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and focused ultrasound have matured considerably over the past two decades. Yet their clinical impact has remained constrained by a fundamental gap: stimulation protocols are rarely informed by the individual’s brain structure and function. Neuroimaging is poised to close that gap. By mapping functional connectivity, cortical excitability, white matter architecture, and network-level dynamics, we can now move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches and toward precision neuromodulation grounded in the living brain’s own organization.
image_alt: Translational brain imaging–guided neuromodulation

title: Virtual Reality for Mental Health: Behavioral Interventions, Therapy, Protocols, and Affective Regulation
summary: Recent advances in immersive technologies have positioned Virtual Reality (VR) as a powerful tool for mental health assessment and intervention. In particular, Virtual Reality Exposure Therapy (VRET) and VR-based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (VR-CBT) have demonstrated effectiveness in treating anxiety disorders, phobias, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). These approaches enable controlled, safe, and ecologically valid environments where emotional and behavioral responses can be elicited, monitored, and modified in real time. Despite promising results, challenges remain in standardizing therapeutic protocols, understanding long-term outcomes, and integrating physiological and behavioral data into adaptive interventions. This Research Topic addresses the need for rigorous, interdisciplinary research that advances VR-based mental health interventions grounded in clinical evidence and behavioral science.

title: After-Work Recovery in Hybrid Work: Remote Work Intensity, Personal Resources, and Recovery Outcomes
summary: The boundaries between work and non-work life have never been more blurred. As hybrid arrangements consolidate as the dominant model in knowledge-intensive sectors, employees increasingly move between professional and personal domains — often within the same physical space. While hybrid work offers autonomy and flexibility, growing evidence suggests it also reshapes the psychological mechanisms through which employees disengage from work, recover from daily demands, and protect their well-being. In this context, the rapid evolution of digital tools and the pervasiveness of communication technologies have introduced new complexities, making individual coping strategies to manage digital demands and psychologically detach from work a critical area of investigation.

title: Edge AI for Robotics: Emerging Technologies and Applications
summary: Edge AI enables AI models to run directly on local devices, bringing computation closer to data sources for faster, more efficient decision-making. Therefore, it is critical for modern robotics, where rapid and robust decision-making is essential. In applications such as high-speed drones and industrial robots operating in extreme conditions, on-device processing ensures real-time control and reliability. Moreover, as service robots become increasingly integrated into daily and personal environments, preserving user privacy during data processing is paramount. While recent advances in AI and deep learning have significantly enhanced robotic capabilities in perception, decision-making, and control, relying solely on cloud-based processing can introduce delays and compromise privacy. Leveraging edge AI enables decentralized, real-time computation that meets the demanding requirements of today's robotic applications.
image_alt: Edge AI for Robotics: Emerging Technologies and Applications

title: Emotional dysregulation, compulsivity, and obsessive-like behaviors across addictions: Neurobiological, psychological, and transdiagnostic perspectives
summary: Emotional dysregulation and compulsivity are widespread but mechanistically underexplored dimensions that cut across substance use disorders, behavioral addictions, and a broader spectrum of maladaptive and addiction-like behaviors. Despite their growing clinical relevance, how these dimensions interact and reinforce one another in self-perpetuating cycles remains insufficiently characterized at both the neurobiological and psychological levels. Alongside emotional dysregulation and compulsivity, obsessive-like behaviors add a further dimension, reflecting the repetitive, intrusive, and rigid action patterns frequently observed across addictive phenotypes, reinforcing their transdiagnostic nature.

title: Executive Function, Shared Intentionality, and Interbrain Synchrony: Cognitive, Embodied and Neural Mechanisms of Joint Attention
summary: In the field of cognitive science, understanding how humans coordinate thought and action with others is central to research on joint attention, shared intentionality, and executive function. Recent advances emphasize the interplay between high-level cognitive mechanisms and neural processes, particularly during real-time social interactions. Despite this progress, critical questions remain regarding the specific neural dynamics enabling shared goals, coordinated attention, and joint action: What are the cognitive and neural bases for linking executive function with shared intentionality? How do oscillatory brain activities support the mechanisms of joint attention, and how does interbrain synchrony reflect interpersonal coordination beyond shared perceptual input? What is the relation between the neural and embodied aspects of the dynamics of joint interaction? title: On the bridge of motor-cognition interaction and robots
summary: Human motor system executes the motor command from high-order regions, rigorously controls the musculoskeletal system and learns to adapt to novel stimuli of dynamic environments. Due to the highly redundant characteristics of the motor system, understanding the optimal and individualized principles of motor control and motor learning is still a scientific challenge. Understanding how brain controls motion and how musculoskeletal system performs commands from the brain and interacts with physical world is a focus for basic science, engineering and clinical translation.

title: In the Shadow of Neurodevelopmental Processes and Media-Digitalism Impacts: The Evolution of Play from Unoccupied Play to Game Design
summary: Liberated from the rules, obligations, and pressures of daily life, yet standing at its very core, play promises absolute freedom and happiness not only to humans but also to animals. Allowing us to become both actor and spectator, play is perhaps the ultimate safe haven where we soothe our existential anxieties. The Vygotskian understanding of play constitutes a central context in which children develop abstract thinking and self-regulation, internalize speech through the transition from social to private and inner speech, and demonstrate their learning potential within the zone of proximal development. Concurrently, through a Piagetian lens, dramatic and imaginative forms of play serve as primary manifestations of cognitive growth, fostering early metacognitive awareness and nurturing the capacity to “think about thinking.” This Research Topic aims to generate actionable insights for early childhood education policies, game-based learning curricula, digital play environment designs,

title: Behavior Change in Climate-Impacted Environments
summary: Weather, climate variability, and extreme environmental conditions can influence when, where, and how people go about their daily behaviors. Heat, rainfall, smoke exposure, and other environmental stressors may disrupt physical activity, sleep, mobility, nutrition and diet, social and work routines, and broader health-related behaviors. At the same time, wearable devices, smartphones, and other digital health tools are creating new opportunities to measure these behavioral responses continuously and at scale.

title: Brain Organization and Behavioral Asymmetries: From Sensory Processing to Cognition Across Species
summary: The two hemispheres of the brain are neither structurally nor functionally symmetrical, and these asymmetries are often reflected in behavior. For more than a century, it was a common but mistaken belief that lateralization was unique to the human brain. However, it is now well established that hemispheric asymmetries are fundamental components of sensory, cognitive, and motor systems across vertebrates and many invertebrates. Behavioral measures such as motor preferences and perceptual biases provide valuable tools for investigating these processes, reflecting links between observable behavior and neural organization. Evidence across taxa also suggests that hemispheric asymmetries may confer evolutionary advantages by enhancing neural efficiency and supporting perceptual, cognitive, and motor performance, with potential benefits for survival.

title: Bridging Brain and Body: Multidisciplinary Perspectives on Exercise and Cognitive Health
summary: The relationship between physical activity and cognitive health has become an important focus in neuroscience, behavioral medicine, and health research. In the context of increasingly sedentary lifestyles and growing cognitive demands, understanding how the body influences the brain is more important than ever. A central concept in this field is neuroplasticity, as physical exercise may induce structural and functional changes in the brain that support cognitive function and resilience against aging and neurological decline.

While DT and the referred parametric structure, are able to build an all-encompassing structured informative models, XR provides the immersive interface for human interaction, defining a dynamic high-fidelity virtual representations of real-world objects. title: Embodied Intelligence for Soft Robots: Proprioception, Perception, Learning, and Control with Advanced Sensing and Actuation
summary: Recent advances in robotics are increasingly driven by the integration of intelligent algorithms, advanced sensing technologies, and novel actuation mechanisms. In particular, the emergence of soft robotics has introduced new opportunities for safe and adaptive interaction with complex environments, enabled by compliant materials and innovative actuation methods e.g., pneumatic actuators. At the same time, progress soft sensor technologies such as optoelectronic sensors has enhanced proprioception capabilities, while machine learning and model predictive control have improved decision-making and system performance. Despite these developments, unifying perception, perception, learning, and control across both rigid and soft robotic systems remains a significant challenge, especially under uncertainty and in dynamic real-world conditions.

Improving Vision-Guided Robotic Systems Through Next-Generation Hand-Eye Calibration Techniques
summary: Robotic vision systems form the foundation of modern industrial automation, enabling high-precision tasks such as assembly, inspection, and object manipulation. Central to their performance is hand-eye calibration, which defines the spatial relationship between the robotic manipulator and the visual sensor. Traditional calibration methods typically rely on multiple feature points, complex mathematical transformations, and iterative optimizations, increasing the risk of cumulative errors and computational inefficiencies. Recent approaches leveraging simplified configurations—such as single fixed feature point methods and algorithms like Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and Levenberg-Marquardt (LM)—have shown promise in reducing setup complexity. However, persistent issues with accuracy, robustness to sensor noise, and adaptability to dynamic environments highlight the need for innovative solutions that balance precision with operational efficiency.

Nutritional neuroscience: How sensory signals influence diet and cognitive function
summary: Despite growing awareness of the role of nutrition in health and cognitive function, the intricate neural mechanisms linking sensory signals and dietary behavior remain underexplored. Sensory cues like taste, smell, and texture significantly influence food preferences, portion control, and satiety, yet how these signals interact with brain regions involved in reward, decision-making, and memory is not fully understood. This gap in knowledge limits our ability to develop effective interventions for nutritional challenges such as obesity, eating disorders, and age-related cognitive decline.

title: Rehabilitation Robotics: Clinical Effectiveness and Patient Engagement
summary: Medical robotics is entering a new phase of development, one in which technological innovation is increasingly expected to translate into meaningful benefits for patients’ recovery, participation, and overall wellbeing. In rehabilitation, robotic systems are no longer viewed only as tools for assistance or repetition, but as part of broader care pathways that can support motivation, autonomy, continuity, and personalized intervention. At the same time, patient engagement has become a central concern in the design and implementation of effective rehabilitation strategies. Advances in wearable and assistive robotics, soft systems, intelligent sensing, remote care, and digital health integration are creating new opportunities to connect physical rehabilitation with more responsive and patient-centered models of support. This Research Topic aims to explore that growing convergence and to highlight contributions that can shape the next generation of rehabilitation-oriented medical robotics.

title: Social Robotics and Artificial Intelligence for Inclusion: Assistive and Interactive Technologies
summary: Social robotics and artificial intelligence are emerging as powerful tools for promoting inclusion and accessibility for people with disabilities. Individuals with cognitive, motor, sensory, or multiple impairments continue to face barriers in education, communication, mobility, employment, and social participation. Advances in socially interactive robots, virtual agents, adaptive AI systems, and intelligent assistive technologies are creating new opportunities to address these challenges, support autonomy, and foster meaningful engagement in learning, care, and everyday activities. Such technologies can support communication, scaffold learning processes, and provide personalized assistance adapted to users’ needs and preferences. At the same time, the deployment of these systems raises important ethical, social, and cultural considerations when applied to vulnerable populations. This Research Topic invites contributions that examine how social robotics and AI can be responsibly design

Diagnosis and Treatment of Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS)
summary: Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) arises from compression of the neurovascular structures passing through the thoracic outlet, and presents across a broad clinical spectrum — from classic neurogenic TOS involving brachial plexus compression, to vascular forms affecting the subclavian artery or vein, to the widely debated “disputed TOS” in which symptoms persist without objective neurological abnormalities. The absence of universally accepted diagnostic criteria has long fueled controversy between neurologists and surgeons, and remains one of the central challenges in managing this condition.

title: Active Mobility in Older Age
summary: Active mobility — encompassing walking, bicycling, and related forms of human-powered transport — offers older adults an accessible route to incorporating physical activity into daily life in an environmentally sustainable way. Worldwide, policies and interventions promote active mobility within the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals framework. Yet, older adults engage in some forms of active mobility less than younger adults, and the psychological processes underlying this difference remain poorly understood. Limited knowledge about bicycling and its benefits, motivation, self-efficacy, fear of falling, social support, age stereotypes, and perceptions of the environment are among the key psychological factors shaping whether older adults take up or maintain active mobility, and whether they benefit from it socially, cognitively, and emotionally. title: Advances in Neural Repair after Stroke: Mechanisms and Clinical Translation
summary: Neural repair after stroke is a vital field focused on addressing persistent disability, which remains common despite progress in acute care. While acute treatments have improved survival and initial outcomes, many stroke survivors face long-term functional deficits due to gaps in repair strategies. Ongoing research has revealed important mechanisms—such as neuroplasticity, axonal sprouting, remyelination, neurogenesis, angiogenesis, and involvement of glial cells, inflammation, and the extracellular matrix—that drive recovery. Although these insights have suggested new avenues for therapy, effective clinical translation and integration of evolving interventions remain major challenges.

title: Human-AI Interaction in Agentic Transportation: Trust, Transparency, and Shared Decision-Making
summary: Advances in AI are giving rise to agentic mobility: intelligent vehicles, in-vehicle agents, automated shuttles, robotaxis, mobility assistants, and connected services that go beyond automating movement to infer user goals, communicate intent, adapt to context, and participate in decisions. These systems function not only as transportation technologies but also as interactive media through which goals, risks, and responsibilities are represented, conveyed, and negotiated. As mobility systems take on these communicative and decision-making roles, the human role shifts from driver and operator toward passenger, supervisor, collaborator, and orchestrator. This transition foregrounds three interrelated challenges for human-media interaction: how trust is established and maintained between people and AI-enabled mobility systems, how the reasoning and limitations of such systems are made transparent to users, and how control and decisions are shared in ways that preserve meaningful human ove
image_alt: Human-AI Interaction in Agentic Transportation: Trust, Transparency, and Shared Decision-Making

title: Modeling, Sensing, Estimation, and Control of Soft and Continuum Robots
summary: Recent progress in materials, flexible sensors, and embedded intelligence has significantly accelerated the development of soft and continuum robots. Compared with conventional rigid robots, these systems offer superior compliance, dexterity, and adaptability but introduce unique challenges in kinematic and dynamic modeling, state estimation, sensing, and control due to their continuously deformable structures and strong nonlinearities. At the same time, emerging technologies such as machine learning, foundation models, digital twins, physics-informed learning, and multimodal perception are creating new opportunities to improve the performance, robustness, and autonomy of these robotic systems. As the field continues to evolve rapidly, there is an increasing need to integrate advances in modeling, estimation, sensing, and control into unified frameworks that enable reliable deployment in real-world applications.
image_alt: Modeling, Sensing, Estimation, and Control of Soft and Continuum Robots

title: Neural and cognitive foundations of human performance and safety in complex engineered systems
summary: The field of human performance in complex engineering systems has emerged at the intersection of neuroscience, cognitive psychology, engineering, and public health. As automation, digitalization, and artificial intelligence transform industries such as transportation, manufacturing, construction, and emergency response, the demands placed on human cognition and physiology have never been greater. Individuals must maintain attention, manage workload, calibrate trust in automation, and make critical decisions under uncertainty—processes that are deeply rooted in neural mechanisms. Recent neurophysiological and cognitive research has provided valuable insights into attentional control, executive functioning, stress responses, and fatigue dynamics that underpin performance and safety outcomes. However, despite advances in neuroimaging and applied cognitive modeling, there remains a gap between mechanistic understanding and its translation into system design, regulatory guidelines, and prev

title: Advances in MRI Radiomics for Non-Invasive Glioma Assessment
summary: Glioma research has rapidly evolved in recent years, particularly in the context of diagnostic imaging and personalized medicine. Gliomas, representing the most prevalent malignant primary brain tumors, are remarkably heterogeneous, posing significant challenges for classification, treatment, and prognosis. While magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains indispensable for diagnosing and monitoring gliomas, traditional visual assessments are often insufficient to uncover the full spectrum of tumor heterogeneity and correlate with underlying molecular features. With advances in computational methods, MRI radiomics has emerged as a transformative approach by extracting large sets of quantitative features from routine imaging, promising to bridge the gap between imaging phenotypes and the molecular landscape of brain tumors.
image_alt: Advances in MRI Radiomics for Non-Invasive Glioma Assessment

title: Brain Resilience: Understanding the Role of Brain, Cognitive, Motor, and Affective Reserves
summary: Brain resilience is a broad term encompassing concepts that seek to explain the brain’s capacity to maintain cognition and effective functioning despite aging, neurological disease, or other forms of adversity. Among the earliest and most influential concepts within this framework are brain reserve and cognitive reserve. Together, these constructs have been used to help explain why the degree of brain pathology does not always correspond directly to the severity of its clinical manifestations.
image_alt: Brain Resilience: Understanding the Role of Brain, Cognitive, Motor, and Affective Reserves

title: The Augmented Human: Exploring the Frontiers of Human Performance Augmentation
summary: The concept of the Augmented Human encompasses various technological solutions that help enhance human performance by supporting the perceptual, cognitive and/or physical capabilities of their users. Recent years have seen a steep growth in this research area, especially when it comes to enhancing human performance using the immersive technology of Augmented Reality (AR) in combination with Artificial Intelligence (AI).

title: The Role of Environmental Stressors in Neurocritical Patient Outcomes: Volume II
summary: Environmental factors play a pivotal role in shaping patient outcomes within neurocritical care, a discipline dedicated to the management of acute and life-threatening neurological conditions. Following the momentum of Volume 1, which explored how climate change influences neurological health and neurocritical management, a broader understanding of environmental stressors has emerged as an urgent frontier. Beyond global climate impacts, acute factors such as hospital air quality, noise levels, light exposure, thermal variability, and stress-inducing surroundings may directly influence pathophysiological mechanisms, neuroinflammation, and neurological recovery. Recent research has highlighted how these physical and psychological stressors contribute to altered cerebral perfusion, metabolic imbalance, and cognitive dysfunction post-injury. Yet, despite growing awareness, empirical evidence connecting modifiable environmental factors to neurological outcomes remains limited, and the integ

title: Early Detection of Cerebral Palsy: From Evidence to Equitable Implementation
summary: Cerebral palsy (CP) is the most common cause of physical disability in childhood worldwide, affecting approximately 1-4 per 1,000 live births, with prevalence significantly higher in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Although the condition is difficult to manage, early diagnosis can help prevent disability caused by the condition. Current international guidelines suggest diagnosis as early as 3-5 months of corrected age, using a combination of General Movements Assessment, Hammersmith Infant Neurological Examination, and magnetic resonance imaging. In high-income countries, early diagnosis of CP has demonstrated feasibility and high acceptability among families and professionals. In contrast, it remains severely underutilized in LMICs, where CP prevalence is higher and clinical presentations more severe.

title: Affordable Cyber-Robotic Systems for Healthcare 5.0
summary: The integration of robots, cyber-physical systems, data-driven control, and artificial intelligence (AI) plays a key role in advancing healthcare delivery and training. Cyber-Robotic Systems (CRS) are robots with intelligent computational and control capabilities that can sense, process, and respond dynamically to the environment. With the rise of data-driven and learning-based control techniques, robotic systems can now operate effectively in environments characterized by uncertainty, variability, and user-specific requirements. This is particularly crucial in areas such as robot-assisted surgery (RAS), rehabilitation, eldercare, and remote diagnostics, where human safety, adaptability, and precision are of top priority. Therefore, CRS can support Healthcare 5.0 which emphasizes personalized care, preventive diagnostics, and patient-focused treatment.

title: Brain–Behavior–Environment Coupling in Neurodevelopment: From Multimodal Mechanisms to Precision Intervention
summary: Neurodevelopment is shaped by dynamic interactions among neural systems, behavioral functions, and environmental contexts. Recent advances in multimodal neuroimaging, computational modeling, and developmental science have highlighted that atypical development—particularly in conditions such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and language impairments—cannot be fully explained by isolated neural deficits. Instead, emerging evidence supports a coupling framework in which brain activity, behavioral adaptation, and environmental input form an integrated system. However, current research remains fragmented across modalities (e.g., EEG, fMRI, eye-tracking) and levels of analysis, limiting our understanding of how these components interact over developmental time and how such interactions can inform targeted interventions.

Optimizing Health and Well-Being Across the Lifespan: A Multidimensional Health Psychology Perspective
summary: Across modern life and work contexts - characterized by uncertainty, complexity, and accelerating demands- sustaining human performance and well-being has become both a psychological and public health priority. Human Performance Optimization (HPO) offers a unifying framework that views optimal functioning as the outcome of dynamic interactions among cognitive, emotional, physical, social, and spiritual domains. Originally rooted in performance-critical settings such as the military, HPO has evolved into a multidimensional approach relevant to healthcare, education, sport, and organizational life. Within health psychology, this paradigm resonates with holistic and positive health models that emphasize resilience, adaptability, and meaning as pillars of sustained human effectiveness and flourishing. Despite growing interest, there remains a need to better understand how these interwoven processes promote lasting well-being and to translate them into evidence-informed practices.

title: Transformations in Work, Workforce, and Workplace: The What, the Who, and the Where of Contemporary Organizations
summary: In an era marked by rapid technological advancements, increasing complexity, and unpredictability, business organizations and the workforce face challenges related to the nature of work, the ways in which work should be performed, and changing labor-force expectations and structures. These challenges serve as drivers of transformation for both organizations and employees in order to remain effective, sustainable, and supportive of well-being. As a result, organizations are rethinking traditional approaches to managing work, employees, and workplaces. Understanding these transformations is essential for addressing the opportunities and challenges associated with the future of work.

title: Carbon-based flexible neural interfaces for multimodal brain activity analysis
summary: Understanding the functionality and complexity of neural networks in the brain represents a significant frontier in neuroscience and neural engineering. Accurate and reliable assessment of neural activities demands innovative implantable devices capable of multimodal measurements over prolonged and varying timescales. Recent advances emphasize the integration of multiple modalities such as electrophysiological recording, neurochemical sensing, imaging, electrical stimulation, and optogenetics to yield richer insights into neuronal dynamics and brain function. Carbon-based flexible neural devices have emerged to address these demands, leveraging materials such as graphene, glassy carbon, boron-doped diamond (BDD), carbon nanotubes (CNTs), and fuzzy graphene. title: Gene–Environment Interplay in the Development of Behavioral and Psychiatric Disorders Across the Lifespan
summary: Behavioral and psychiatric disorders arise from dynamic interactions between genetic predisposition and environmental influences across development and aging. Increasing evidence highlights critical windows of vulnerability and plasticity during which environmental exposures—such as early-life stress, social context, nutrition, and age-related physiological changes—shape genetic risk. Advances in human genetics, longitudinal cohort studies, and multi-omics approaches, alongside mechanistic investigations in model organisms (e.g., rodents, zebrafish, and invertebrates), have provided new insights into conserved developmental pathways regulating behavior and psychiatric traits.

title: The Development of Aggression in Children and Adolescents in the Digital Era
summary: The digital technology has profoundly transformed the social interaction patterns of children and adolescents, and has also given rise to new forms and developmental pathways of aggression. Issues such as cyberbullying, toxic behaviors, and social media conflicts are increasingly prominent, with aggressive behaviors no longer confined to real life but extending into the virtual world. Problematic internet use (e.g., gaming, short videos, social media, artificial intelligence) and exposure to adverse media factors (e.g., violence, competition) may exert significant effects on various types of aggression. Currently, there is a lack of systematic integration regarding the dynamic trajectories, typological differentiation, and psychological and physiological mechanisms of aggression development in the digital era. title: Exploring autonomic regulation in maternal mental health: Physiological pathways underlying pregnancy, stress, and neonatal outcomes
summary: The field of autonomic neuroscience provides a powerful framework to understand how physiological regulation underlies maternal mental health and perinatal adaptation. During pregnancy and the postpartum period, autonomic, neuroendocrine, and immune systems interact dynamically to maintain homeostasis in the face of emotional and physiological experiences and challenges. Maternal mental health conditions — including perinatal depression, anxiety, and stress-related conditions — have been increasingly recognized as significant contributors to adverse outcomes for both mothers and their infants. However, the underlying autonomic mechanisms that link psychological states to biological function remain insufficiently explored. Recent studies highlight that alterations in heart rate variability, vagal tone, and sympathetic–parasympathetic balance reflect the degree of stress adaptation and may predict emotional states, resilience, and perinatal outcomes. title: From Synapses to Silicon: Theoretical Foundations and Neuromorphic Implementations of Biological Learning
summary: Learning in biological neural systems emerges from the coordinated interaction of molecular, cellular, and circuit-level mechanisms that collectively give rise to adaptive behavior across timescales spanning milliseconds to years. At the most elementary level, synaptic efficacy is dynamically regulated through activity-dependent processes, including voltage- and calcium-mediated long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD), spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), and metaplasticity. These local synaptic rules, however, do not operate in isolation: neuromodulatory systems impose global signals that gate plasticity, encode reward prediction errors, and regulate the transition between exploratory and consolidative learning states. The age range of patients and their underlying conditions vary widely, as does the outcome. Neurological and developmental follow-up care for children after MCS is not yet systematic and structured in many countries. Current guidelines therefore recommend the establishment of follow-up programs. The establishment of these programs should be adapted to the circumstances of the respective countries, cultures, families and patients. title: Mental Health Across the Academic Career: Predictors, Protective Factors, and Intervention Strategies
summary: Academia is a demanding environment where students, doctoral candidates, and researchers may experience academic pressure, competitive evaluation, precarious career pathways, publishing demands, isolation, financial insecurity, and challenges associated with international mobility or caregiving responsibilities. Research indicates elevated levels of distress and burnout among different academic populations, particularly postgraduate and early-career researchers, although prevalence and risk vary across disciplines, countries, career stages, and social groups. Mental health in academia can be shaped by the interaction of individual characteristics, supervisory and peer relationships, workload, organizational cultures, and wider sociocultural influences. title: Methods in Molecular Neuroscience
summary: Progress in molecular neuroscience depends as much on the questions we ask as on the tools we have to answer them. Over the past decade, the field has gained access to a remarkable set of methods that allow researchers to probe brain function with cellular and molecular precision, across systems ranging from invertebrates to brain organoids and human induced pluripotent stem cells. Genetic engineering, optogenetics and chemogenetics, advanced imaging, biosensors, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, proteomics, behavioral assays, and bioinformatics now form the methodological backbone of work across the entire spectrum of molecular neuroscience, from basic signaling pathways to disease mechanisms, plasticity, and pain.

title: Microglia, Neuroinflammation, and Neurodegeneration in Brain Aging and Age-Associated Disease
summary: Aging of the central nervous system is characterized by intricate changes in immune regulation, molecular signaling, and neuronal integrity. Among the key players in this process are microglia, the resident immune cells of the brain, whose fundamental role in maintaining tissue homeostasis becomes progressively impaired with advancing age. Evidence from preclinical and clinical studies indicates that microglial dysfunction contributes to chronic low-grade neuroinflammation, synaptic deterioration, and neuronal loss; hallmarks of neurodegenerative pathologies such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and other forms of dementia. Despite major advances in understanding these associations, significant gaps persist regarding how microglial state transitions, metabolic reprogramming, and regional heterogeneity shape disease progression and resilience. title: Modeling Sensory Encoding: Computational Approaches to Feature Detection, Integration, and Adaptation
summary: Sensory encoding is the vital process by which the nervous system transforms physical stimuli into meaningful neural representations. Traditionally, computational neuroscience has characterized this through receptive fields and stimulus-response functions. However, sensory systems do not operate in a vacuum; they must extract relevant features from high-dimensional, noisy environments while constantly adjusting to changing contexts. From the retina’s light adaptation to the auditory system’s frequency tuning, the brain employs sophisticated computational strategies to ensure efficient information transmission. As our ability to record from large sensory populations grows, we are moving beyond simple linear models toward theories that encompass non-linear dynamics, population-level interactions, and the influence of feedback. Understanding these principles is essential for deciphering how the brain constructs a coherent internal map of the external world.

Mapping Pathways to Suicide Risk in Young Adults: Quarter-Life Crisis and NEET Experiences
summary: Suicide is one of the leading causes of death among people aged 15–29 worldwide. For many young people, suicidal thoughts and behaviours develop during the transition into adulthood, a period that is often associated with important decisions about education, work, relationships, housing and identity. Increasingly, these transitions are becoming longer, less predictable and more difficult to navigate. Some young people feel unable to move into the adult roles they want, while others feel trapped in commitments or circumstances that no longer suit them. These experiences are often described as the “locked-out” and “locked-in” forms of quarter-life crisis. They may contribute to feelings of defeat, entrapment, hopelessness, loneliness and a lack of belonging. Young people who are not in education, employment or training (NEET) may face similar challenges, including loss of routine, financial insecurity, social isolation and reduced contact with support services. title: Adaptive Human-Robot Collaboration in Smart Manufacturing: Cognitive Feedback, Dynamic Task Allocation, and Industry 5.0 Integration
summary: The transition toward Industry 5.0 places human wellbeing and operator-centred design at the core of advanced manufacturing systems. Collaborative robots (cobots) are no longer simply tools for automation, they are partners in dynamic, shared workspaces where safety, adaptability, and trust must be continuously negotiated in real time.

title: Edge-Deployed Generative AI for Context-Aware Decision Support in Wearable Robotic Systems
summary: Recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), have transformed how machines interpret, reason, and communicate. At the same time, robotics research has made significant progress in edge computing, sensor fusion, and real-time perception systems, enabling deployment in dynamic and resource-constrained environments. Despite these developments, a critical gap remains in the integration of generative AI with embodied robotic systems operating at the edge, especially in wearable robotics such as smart helmets, assistive devices, and human-augmentation systems. Current research topics emphasise either cloud-based intelligence or isolated edge AI solutions, but lack a unified framework for real-time, context-aware decision support that combines perception, reasoning, and action under strict computational constraints.

title: Effort, Attention, and Arousal: Brain–Body Mechanisms for Performance in the Real World
summary: Sustained performance in high-stakes, real-world environments places extraordinary demands on the human brain and body. Effort, attention, and arousal are three tightly interwoven constructs that together govern how individuals mobilize cognitive and physiological resources to meet these demands. Nowhere is this more critical than in contexts in which humans are expected to perform in high stakes environments. For example, military personnel, first responders, and individuals of the like must maintain peak cognitive performance under conditions of extreme stress, fatigue, sensory overload, and physical exertion. Despite decades of laboratory research, the neural and peripheral mechanisms underpinning the interaction between mental effort, attentional control, and arousal remain incompletely understood — particularly in the demanding and ecologically complex environments that are present in real-world scenarios.

title: From Mechanism to Management: Neuropsychological, Neurobiological, and Psychopathological Foundations of Geriatric Psychiatric Care
summary: Geriatric psychiatry sits at the intersection of neuroscience, psychology, and clinical medicine, addressing the complex mental health challenges that accompany aging. Older adults often present with multifactorial conditions, including depression, anxiety, cognitive decline, psychotic symptoms, medication effects, and sleep disruption, that rarely conform to a single explanatory level. Recent research highlights complex interactions among neurobiological changes, psychopathological presentations, psychopharmacological treatments, and psychosocial variables such as loneliness and autonomy. Despite growing evidence, clinical care models often remain fragmented, with limited integration between neuropsychological assessment, biological mechanisms, and treatment approaches. This integration gap underscores the need for a translational, multidisciplinary framework spanning the continuum from neuropsychological and neurobiological mechanisms to psychopathology and treatment in later life.

title: Predictive motor control and internal models
summary: Skilled motor behaviour relies on the central nervous system’s capacity to predict, rather than merely react to, the sensory consequences of its own actions. From reaching for a cup of coffee to maintaining balance on a moving train, every voluntary movement relies on the central nervous system’s ability to anticipate the sensory consequences of its own actions. This predictive capacity is thought to be supported by internal models: neural representations of the body and the external world that allow the brain to estimate forthcoming states and select appropriate motor commands. Forward models predict the sensory outcomes of motor actions, while inverse models compute the motor commands required to achieve a desired sensory or kinematic goal. Together, they form the computational backbone of skilled, flexible, and adaptive behaviour, and their disruption is increasingly recognised as a hallmark of several neurological and psychiatric conditions.
image_alt: Predictive motor control and internal models

title: Psychological Factors in Physical Education and Sport - Volume VIII
Push the System: Stimulation, Pharmacology, and Closed-Loop Tests of Cognitive Mechanisms
summary: Cognitive processes such as attention, perception, memory, executive function, and social cognition emerge from dynamic interactions between distributed neural systems. While correlational methods like neuroimaging and electrophysiology have mapped these networks extensively, they cannot establish whether a given neural signature is necessary or sufficient for a cognitive function. Causal interventions—including non-invasive brain stimulation (TMS, tDCS, tACS), pharmacological manipulation, and closed-loop neurofeedback systems—offer a powerful complement, allowing researchers to directly perturb neural systems and observe the behavioral consequences. Advances in real-time signal processing and adaptive stimulation now make it possible to test cognitive theories with unprecedented precision and mechanistic specificity.

title: Shedding light on Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) Vol II
summary: Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (CFS), also called Myalgic Encephalomyelitis (ME) is a disabling neurological condition affecting millions of people worldwide. ME/CFS is characterized by persistent and unexplained fatigue, post-exertional malaise, cognitive impairments, and a range of other symptoms such as pain, sleep disturbances, and gastrointestinal issues. Despite the significant impact on patients' lives and the number of sufferers, ME/CFS remains poorly understood, stigmatized, and lacks effective treatments.

title: Young Brains at Play: Advances in Pediatric Sports Concussion
summary: Sports-related concussions represent one of the most common injuries in children and adolescents participating in organized athletics. Each year, thousands of pediatric athletes worldwide experience concussive events, with the actual incidence likely underestimated due to underreporting and variances in awareness and diagnostic practices. Pediatric athletes are not simply “small adults”; their developing brains, unique biomechanics, and evolving cognitive and emotional profiles demand specialized approaches that consider both immediate safety and lifelong neurological health. This collection serves as a platform for multidisciplinary voices to address the complex medical, scientific, and societal challenges surrounding pediatric sports concussion.

Emerging evidence suggests that maternal factors during pregnancy — including physical activity, nutrition, stress, and metabolic and immune profiles — play a crucial role in shaping the offspring’s neuropsychological outcomes. However, the precise cognitive, behavioral, and emotional consequences of these prenatal influences, and the brain pathways that underlie them, have yet to be fully elucidated.

summary: Children and adolescents are growing up in an environment saturated with screens. Smartphones, tablets, gaming consoles, and social media platforms now shape how young people learn, socialize, and regulate emotion, often from the first years of life. As recreational and educational screen use continues to climb, parents, educators, clinicians, and public health authorities are asking urgent questions about what this means for the developing brain. A growing body of evidence links excessive or poorly contextualized screen exposure to changes in attention, executive function, language acquisition, sleep, and socio-emotional regulation. At the same time, screens can support learning, connection, and access to health information when used well. The picture is further complicated for children with, or at risk of, neurodevelopmental conditions such as ADHD and autism spectrum disorder, where screen use patterns may both reflect and reinforce underlying vulnerabilities. title: Edge-AI Sensor Fusion for UAV-Based Perception in Large-Scale Surveillance and Environmental Monitoring
summary: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) equipped with multi-sensor payloads (cameras, LiDAR, multispectral and thermal imagers) are increasingly deployed for large-scale surveillance and environmental monitoring, from infrastructure inspection to crop health assessment and wildlife tracking. These deployments generate large volumes of heterogeneous sensor data that must be processed reliably, often with limited onboard compute and intermittent connectivity to centralized systems. Edge-AI addresses this by moving perception and decision-making closer to the sensor, reducing latency and bandwidth demands while enabling real-time response in the field. Achieving robust perception under these conditions requires effective fusion of multiple sensor modalities, lightweight models suited to onboard hardware, and architectures that remain reliable across varied, often unpredictable environments.

title: Computational and Theoretical Approaches to Autism: From Neural Mechanisms to Behavior
summary: Marking World Autism Awareness Day 2026, this Research Topic aims to bring together computational, theoretical, and data-driven studies that advance a mechanistic understanding of autism across multiple levels of analysis, from synaptic and circuit-level processes to large-scale brain dynamics, cognition, and behavior.

title: Female Genital Mutilation/Cutting: Addressing the Evidence Gaps
summary: Female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C) is a serious, widespread and persistent threat to the health of women, girls, and communities worldwide. Existing evidence about FGM/C’s drivers, risk factors, epidemiologic profile, and health complications are well documented. However, there are areas of inquiry that remain under-explored in current evidence, limiting governments, institutions, and donors’ ability to make progress in both preventing the practice and improving the quality of life for people with FGM/C. This collection aims to address the specific gaps detailed below by focusing on under-explored areas of inquiry related to FGM/C, including life-course and social determinants perspectives.

title: Neurobiology of stress and resilience: Mechanisms and coping strategies from a Human Neuroscience perspective, Volume II
summary: The experience of stress is an inevitable part of human life, affecting individuals physically, emotionally, and psychologically. From brief tension-filled moments to chronic stress exposure, the resulting impact on the human brain is profound, influencing neural circuits and even altering brain function. Despite its potential detriments, stress also presents an opportunity for resilience—an adaptive response enabling individuals to maintain mental health despite adversity. This area of research is crucial for advancing our understanding of how resilience is cultivated and how stress can be managed effectively to prevent stress-related disorders. The field of human neuroscience offers valuable insights into the underlying biological mechanisms that govern stress responses and resilience building.

summary: In recent years, numerous developments have taken place in the field of neuromodulation. The introduction of newer technologies, software and increasing understanding of brain physiology in neurological and psychiatric conditions have shaped this rapidly growing field. To create a space where all stakeholders could freely interact to discuss challenges, advancements and opportunities in the field, the first Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) Think Tank took place in 2012 in Gainesville Florida at the University of Florida. Since then, the meeting has grown to a hybrid virtual and in person meeting expanding the number of participants to over 200 world experts in the field.

Synergizing Morphological Development and Learning in Robotics: New Frontiers for Embodied Intelligence
summary: The field of embodied robotics has experienced a significant paradigm shift toward understanding how a robot’s physical structure (morphology) and its adaptive control mechanisms (learning) co-evolve to produce intelligent behaviors. Traditional approaches have often treated morphology and learning as separate design components, but recent perspectives emphasize that their interaction is essential for achieving higher levels of autonomy and adaptability. Studies inspired by natural developmental processes have demonstrated the potential of integrated developmental strategies in improving robot performance across dynamic tasks. However, key conflicts remain unresolved. title: Transdiagnostic affective neuroscience: from negative affect to anhedonia and cognitive control.
summary: Research in psychiatry and clinical neuroscience is increasingly recognizing that negative affect and anhedonia are not confined to a single diagnostic category. Traditionally, most research on these symptoms has been conducted within single-diagnosis frameworks, treating depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia spectrum disorders, and anxiety-related conditions as largely separate research literatures. This separation limits understanding of the shared neural and cognitive mechanisms that link reduced positive affect to impaired cognitive control across conditions. While several studies have pointed to overlapping reward and executive control circuits across diagnoses, critical questions remain about how these mechanisms interact, whether they follow a common trajectory, and how they can be reliably measured and targeted for intervention. title: Machine Learning and Observational Data for Clinical Trial Optimization
summary: Clinical research has long rested on a familiar triad: the randomized trial, the carefully curated cohort, and the cross-sectional survey. Each has its strengths, and each has its blind spots. Trials give us causality but often at great cost and with narrow generalizability. Cohorts offer longitudinal depth but can suffer from attrition and evolving practice patterns. Surveys provide breadth and currency but limited temporal insight. For decades, these data streams have largely run in parallel, occasionally informing one another but rarely being analyzed together with the tools now at our disposal.

summary: Over the past decade, social robotics and affective AI have emerged as promising tools in educational and therapeutic contexts. Studies have shown that socially interactive robots can enhance engagement, motivation, and learning outcomes for both typically developing learners and neurodiverse populations. At the same time, advances in AI - including multimodal sensing, emotion recognition, attention tracking, and adaptive interaction - have enabled robots to provide more personalized and responsive educational support. The degree of robot embodiment, and in particular the use of humanoid robots, has been shown to play a meaningful role in shaping the quality and nature of human-robot interaction, with implications for engagement and learning. However, much of the existing research remains limited to controlled laboratory environments, reducing ecological validity and limiting translation into everyday educational practice. title: Aging brain: Brain health and neuroprotective strategies, Volume II
summary: As global life expectancy continues to rise, understanding the complexities of the aging brain has become increasingly critical. Aging, while a natural process, brings about structural and functional changes in the brain that can affect cognitive health and overall neurological function. These changes can lead to age-related cognitive decline and an increased risk of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. Research in this area is crucial to unraveling the mechanisms that drive these changes and identifying the factors that can help maintain brain health and functionality throughout aging.

title: CNS Immune Cell Compartmentalization and Neuroinflammation
summary: Neuroimmunology has demonstrated that T cells residing in the human brain constitute a distinct, tissue-adapted lymphocyte population. Unlike their circulating counterparts, these resident T cells exist within a highly regulated and privileged central nervous system (CNS) environment. A surge in the availability of post-mortem brain tissue, alongside powerful omics and neuroimaging tools, has begun to clarify the unique attributes and behaviors of CNS-resident lymphocytes. In conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS), there is mounting evidence that these populations do not merely infiltrate the CNS during acute inflammation but occupy specialized niches—most notably within the meninges and perivascular spaces—and interact closely with resident B cells and myeloid cells. Despite advances using both human samples and animal models, fundamental questions remain regarding the precise mechanisms of lymphocyte compartmentalization, their residency programs, and their persistent role in MS

title: Circadian–Melatonin Axis in Systemic Disease: From Molecular Mechanisms to Precision Medicine
summary: The circadian system orchestrates physiological processes across multiple organ systems, maintaining homeostasis through tightly regulated molecular clocks. As a primary endocrine signal, melatonin plays a pivotal role in synchronizing circadian rhythms with environmental cues and modulating diverse biological functions, including metabolism, immune surveillance, and cellular stress adaptation.

title: Climate Change, Emerging Pollutant Exposure and Mental Health
summary: Climate change and emerging environmental pollutants are increasingly recognized as critical determinants of mental health worldwide. Rapid urbanization, rising ambient temperatures, and extreme weather events have been associated with elevated risks of depression, anxiety, sleep disturbances, and other neuropsychiatric outcomes. At the same time, exposure to emerging pollutants, including microplastics, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), endocrine-disrupting chemicals, artificial light at night (ALAN), and novel airborne contaminants, may adversely affect brain and mental health through pathways involving neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, endocrine disruption, circadian dysregulation, and alterations in brain structure or functional connectivity. Although growing evidence supports the independent effects of climate-related stressors and pollutant exposures on mental health, their combined and interactive impacts remain insufficiently understood. However, understanding the critical challenges and taking advantage of the potential of these tools for educational practices can often be limited by educators’ and students’ low levels of AI literacy. title: Gut-Brain Axis: Microbiota’s Role in Neuroimmunological Disorders
summary: The gut-brain axis represents a dynamic, bidirectional communication network connecting the gastrointestinal (GI) tract to the central nervous system (CNS), with the microbiota playing a pivotal role in modulating neurological and immunological processes. Recent advances have uncovered intricate pathways by which the intestinal microbiome can influence CNS homeostasis and contribute to the development or progression of various neuroimmunological and neurodegenerative disorders. While compelling correlations have been established between gut dysbiosis and diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, and neuropathic pain, the precise causal mechanisms remain only partially understood. Current research points to gut microbial metabolites, immune system cross-talk, and systemic inflammation as critical mediators driving CNS inflammation and autoimmune responses. title: Integrative Perspectives on CSF Biomarkers in the Phenotyping and Management of Multiple Sclerosis
summary: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis has long been an essential tool in the study and management of neurological diseases, particularly multiple sclerosis (MS). While the presence of CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands has historically played a role in MS diagnosis, emerging biomarkers such as kappa-neurofilament light chains and brain-specific proteins are increasingly recognized for their value in characterizing disease activity, predicting progression, and understanding underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. Despite significant advances, ambiguity remains in differentiating MS phenotypes and forecasting individual patient trajectories. Critical areas of debate persist regarding the specificity, sensitivity, and prognostic utility of a range of CSF biomarkers, as well as their utility in evaluating treatment response and disease modification. title: Intelligent Manipulation of Space Robots: Environmental Perception, Autonomous Decision-Making, and Dexterous Operations
summary: Space robots are becoming indispensable for next-generation space missions, including on-orbit servicing, station maintenance, spacecraft inspection, debris removal, and planetary exploration. These missions require robots to operate in unattended, safety-critical, and highly uncertain space environments. Non-cooperative targets, complex contact conditions, changing illumination, communication delay, limited onboard resources, and microgravity-induced coupling impose major challenges on environmental perception, motion planning, and closed-loop control. These characteristics make traditional operation modes based on ground planning and predefined trajectories insufficient for demanding on-orbit tasks. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, learning-based control, multi-sensor fusion, and digital twin technology offer promising pathways toward autonomous, dexterous manipulation in space. title: Legal and ethical reforms for neurotechnological advancements in the global south: perspective and challenges, Volume II
summary: Advancements in neurotechnology are heralding new possibilities for enhancing human health and cognitive abilities. However, these innovations also bring to the fore significant ethical, legal, and social challenges, particularly in the spheres of mental privacy and autonomy. Traditionally, the discourse on neuroethics has been shaped by perspectives from the global North, often overlooking the distinct socio-economic and cultural contexts of countries in the global South. These white spots in neuroethical deliberations are critical, seeing as these regions grapple with unique challenges such as high income inequality, limited healthcare infrastructure, and significant linguistic and cultural diversity.

title: Mental Health and Resilience in Aging Populations: Insurance Systems, Risk Factors, and Public Health Strategies
summary: Population aging is one of the defining public health challenges of this century: by 2050, the global population aged 60 and older will nearly double, and mental health conditions—particularly depression, anxiety, and social isolation—remain among the most under-recognized and under-treated health burdens in this group. The World Health Organization estimates that a significant share of older adults experience a mental or neurological disorder, yet mental health services for this population remain fragmented, underfunded, and inconsistently integrated with physical health care. A structural factor underlying much of this fragmentation has received comparatively little research attention: the design of health and long-term care insurance systems, which shapes who can access mental health services, at what cost, and with what downstream effect on care utilization and caregiver wellbeing. title: Metastatic Niches Uncovered: Organ-Specific Mechanisms Driving Brain, Bone, Lung, and Liver Metastases
summary: Metastasis remains the leading cause of cancer-related death, yet therapeutic progress continues to lag behind advances in our understanding of primary tumor biology. Growing evidence shows that metastatic spread is not a uniform process but is heavily influenced by organ-specific microenvironments, or metastatic “niches.” Unique biological, immunological, and metabolic characteristics within the brain, bone, lung, and liver actively affect tumor colonization, survival, and growth.

summary: The interplay between diet, the gut microbiome, and brain function has emerged as a promising frontier in neuropharmacology. Increasing evidence indicates that food-derived bioactive compounds and psychobiotics (beneficial microorganisms strains capable of synthesizing and delivering neuroactive compounds that act through the gut–brain axis) can influence neurotransmission, neuroinflammation, neuroplasticity, and the gut–brain axis. These findings highlight the potential of nutritional and microbial interventions as complementary or alternative approaches to support mood regulation, cognitive function, and emotional well-being. Unlike traditional pharmacological treatments, which often carry side effects or limited long-term efficacy, food-based and microbiome-targeted strategies may provide safe, accessible, and sustainable avenues for mental health promotion. title: Thriving While Work Is Rewritten: Innovation and Sustainable Work in the Adjacent Possible
summary: Work is being rewritten on several fronts at once, by technological developments such as digitalisation and generative AI, by organisational changes such as algorithmic management and hybrid work, and by broader societal pressures including sustainability demands and demographic change. These changes do not merely introduce new tools or procedures; they reshape expectations, relationships, employment lifecycles, opportunities, and constraints within organisations. This Research Topic adopts the lens of the adjacent possible to explore how innovation in work design, organisational processes, and structures unfolds from what already exists, opening new pathways for action, adaptation, and development while also generating new tensions, risks, and inequalities. At the centre of the Topic is the question of thriving, whether and under what conditions people and organisations can flourish rather than merely cope as work is reconfigured.

summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significant potential to transform neurology by enhancing the diagnosis and treatment of brain diseases. Current tools use AI for accurate epilepsy diagnosis, brain mapping, and surgical planning. AI can analyze large data volumes, explore biomarkers clinicians might miss, and improve diagnosis and treatment accuracy. Machine learning algorithms can process extensive data sets and patient information, developing accurate models for diagnosis and treatment. AI can identify unique, unbiased patterns in data, potentially discovering new biomarkers or intervention methods. These AI-driven systems are faster and more efficient than manual processes. Furthermore, AI can aid in developing new treatments for neurological disorders like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's and create personalized treatment plans based on individual neurological profiles.
