title: AI-Driven Analysis of Electrodermal and Multimodal Biosignals for Autonomic and Neurocognitive State Monitoring
summary: The autonomic nervous system and the brain interact continuously to shape emotional, cognitive, and physiological states. Electrodermal activity (EDA), long recognized as a sensitive marker of sympathetic arousal, is now increasingly paired with EEG, fNIRS, and other neural signals to build richer, AI-driven models of autonomic-neural function. Advances in machine learning, deep learning, and nonlinear signal processing have made it possible to extract subtle, previously inaccessible patterns from these biosignals — enabling new tools for stress detection, pain assessment, cognitive workload estimation, sleep and arousal monitoring, and early detection of autonomic or neurocognitive dysfunction.

title: Affective Computing Meets Embodied Intelligence: Emotion Perception, Reasoning, and Interaction in Embodied Agents
summary: Affective computing aims to endow machines with the ability to recognize, interpret, and respond to human emotions, while embodied intelligence emphasizes that cognition emerges through an agent's physical interaction with its environment. Historically, these two fields have advanced along largely separate trajectories: affective computing has focused on emotion recognition from facial, vocal, physiological, and textual signals, whereas embodied intelligence has concentrated on perception, control, and manipulation in the physical world. Recent breakthroughs in large multimodal models, foundation models for robotics, and human-robot interaction have created unprecedented opportunities to unify the two. Emotion is no longer treated as a passive signal to be classified, but as an active component that shapes how embodied agents perceive, reason, decide, and act within dynamic, socially rich environments.

title: Restoring Sensation and Perception: From neural coding to adaptive neurotechnology
summary: Sensation and perception arise from complex neural processes through which the human brain encodes, integrates, interprets, and adapts to information from the external environment and the body. Disruption of these processes can result from sensory loss, stroke, traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury, neurodegenerative disorders, chronic pain, and other neurological conditions, substantially impairing communication, mobility, independence, and quality of life. At the same time, rapid advances in neural recording, computational modelling, brain–computer interfaces, neuroprosthetics, artificial intelligence, and adaptive neuromodulation are creating new opportunities to restore, substitute, or rehabilitate sensory and perceptual functions.

title: Emergency Psychiatry and Mental Health: Current Challenges, Innovations, and Pathways to Care
summary: Psychiatric emergencies represent a critical and growing challenge for health systems worldwide. The rising demand for emergency mental health services—driven by factors such as the COVID-19 pandemic, socioeconomic stressors, and reduced access to community-based care—has placed unprecedented pressure on emergency departments, crisis teams, and acute inpatient services. Despite this, emergency psychiatry remains an under-researched and often fragmented field, with significant gaps in evidence-based assessment, intervention, and care coordination.

The cortical representation of speech and auditory perception: current developments, Vol II
summary: The interaction between speech and auditory perception and the brain’s cortical activity remains an important area of study in neuroscience. Speech and auditory perception, essential components of human communication and environmental awareness, involve the processing of sounds, neural activities, and interpretation. Understanding how the brain deciphers and makes sense of speech and auditory stimuli is crucial for cognitive neuroscience and has practical applications in treating speech and hearing disorders and improving speech recognition technology.

title: Trustworthy Neurological AI: Evidence Standards from Validation to Clinical Deployment
summary: Artificial intelligence is now being investigated across much of clinical neurology, including EEG interpretation, seizure detection, stroke imaging, neurodegenerative disease classification, neurocritical care monitoring, and clinical decision support. Many studies report high performance using metrics such as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, or area under the ROC curve. Yet the number of systems with robust evidence of real-world clinical benefit remains comparatively small. This translational gap reflects recurrent methodological and implementation problems: reliance on narrowly characterized public datasets, limited demographic and technical diversity, insufficient external validation, incomplete calibration assessment, and evaluation strategies that do not map onto clinically meaningful decisions.

title: Understanding Cognitive and Executive Functioning in Neurodevelopmental Disorders: A focus on Cognitive, Social, and Inclusion Perspectives in Real-World Contexts
summary: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), intellectual disability, and specific learning disorders, are characterized by early-onset differences in cognitive, behavioral, and social functioning. While substantial advances have been made in identifying neurobiological and cognitive mechanisms, significant gaps remain in understanding how these conditions unfold across real-world contexts—particularly within families, schools, and communities.

title: Biophysics and artificial intelligence: convergent approaches to characterize pathological protein aggregates in neurodegeneration
summary: To understand what has gone wrong in a neurodegenerative disease, one must first establish what is actually different. In many disorders, that difference is carried by the protein assemblies themselves: the same polypeptide arranged into a distinct conformer, polymorph, oligomeric state, or kinetic species. Detecting and quantifying these differences is therefore not a preliminary step, but the foundation on which mechanistic understanding, neuropathological marker development, and therapeutic strategies all rest. Before anything else, it is an analytical problem.

title: Toward Lifelong Autonomy: Advancing Continual Robot Learning for Adaptable Intelligent Systems
summary: Continual robot learning is an emerging interdisciplinary field that integrates advances from machine learning, robotics, and cognitive science to build agents capable of accumulating knowledge and skills throughout their lifetime. Unlike traditional training paradigms that assume static objectives, continual learning examines how robots can learn new tasks drawn from an evolving, potentially unbounded distribution. The key challenge lies in balancing stability and plasticity—learning new behaviours efficiently while retaining previously acquired competencies. Foundations from continual learning research have introduced three main families of methods: (1) regularization-based strategies that constrain updates to preserve past knowledge, (2) replay-based approaches that revisit experience memories to prevent forgetting, and (3) dynamic architectures that allocate specific model capacity to emerging tasks. title: Advancing Stroke Rehabilitation through Neuromodulation and Brain-Computer Interface Innovation
summary: Stroke ranks as the leading cause of adult disability globally. Post-stroke motor, cognitive, language and emotional deficits greatly impede patients’ recovery of activities of daily living (ADL). Driven by interdisciplinary progress in brain science, engineering medicine and neuroscience, targeted central neuromodulation and human-computer interactive brain-computer interfaces (BCI) have evolved as pivotal frontier strategies to facilitate post-stroke brain plasticity and overcome rehabilitation limitations for refractory post-stroke sequela.

Disorders of motor circuit function: dystonia, ataxia, tremor, spasticity, and tic disorders
summary: Motor circuit disorders represent a heterogeneous group of neurological conditions characterised by disruptions in the neural pathways governing voluntary and involuntary movement. Dystonia, ataxia, spasticity, and tic disorders — despite their distinct clinical presentations — share common threads in their underlying pathophysiology, involving dysfunction across cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical and cerebellar circuits. Advances in neuroimaging, electrophysiology, genetics, and neuromodulation have significantly expanded our understanding of these conditions, yet many questions remain regarding their mechanisms, progression, and optimal management.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Deep Learning Innovations for Sustainable Aquaculture and Underwater Environments
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning are emerging as transformative forces in the modern landscape of aquaculture and underwater environmental management. This rapidly evolving field has redefined best practices, equipping researchers and aquaculture practitioners with powerful tools for automating complex processes, enhancing the precision of biomass estimation, and enabling comprehensive monitoring of aquatic and marine environments. Recent breakthroughs demonstrate how state-of-the-art neural network architectures, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformer-based models, are overcoming traditional constraints in underwater visual analysis ranging from turbidity and poor illumination to multi-species differentiation and challenging habitat complexity. The integration of AI with intelligent sensor networks and robotics is not only boosting operational efficiency but also advancing sustainability, animal welfare, and ecosystem resilience at a time when globa

title: Beyond Symptom Control - Mechanistic Lessons from Failed and Emerging Disease-Modifying Therapies in Parkinson’s Disease
summary: Parkinson’s disease (PD) remains the second most common neurodegenerative disorder worldwide, yet despite decades of mechanistic insight, every clinical trial of a disease-modifying therapy (DMT) to date has failed to deliver unequivocal evidence of slowed neurodegeneration. Recent high-profile negative results — including trials of NLY01 (a GLP-1 receptor agonist targeting microglial activation) and deferiprone (an iron chelator targeting nigral iron accumulation and ferroptotic vulnerability) — have prompted a critical re-examination of the preclinical models, target validation strategies, and molecular hypotheses that underpin the DMT pipeline.

title: Cortical Plasticity in Retinal Disease: Mechanisms of Reorganization following Vision Loss
summary: Retinal disease, whether caused by age-related macular degeneration, retinitis pigmentosa, inherited macular and cone–rod dystrophies, or diabetic retinopathy, was long thought to leave the visual cortex it deprives essentially silent. Over the past two decades, that view has been overturned: neurons formerly driven by the lesioned retina begin responding to stimulation from surrounding, intact regions, receptive-field properties shift, and measurable functional and structural remodeling emerges across the visual pathway. Understanding the mechanisms, limits, and behavioral consequences of this plasticity is now central to both basic visual neuroscience and the design of restorative and rehabilitative therapies.

title: Engineered In Vitro Platforms to Probe Neural Circuit Dysfunction in CNS Disorders
summary: Disorders of the central nervous system (CNS) - including neurodegenerative, neurodevelopmental, and neuropsychiatric conditions - arise from complex alterations in neuronal and glial function, synaptic communication, and circuit organization. Despite major advances in molecular neuroscience, how cellular dysfunction develops into aberrant network activity remains poorly understood, and conventional models often fail to reproduce human neural circuitry, cellular diversity, and patient-specific pathophysiology. Meeting this challenge requires new neurotechnologies capable of building and interrogating human neural circuits in vitro.

title: Impact of rare disease genes on neural development and function
summary: Rare disease genes, though individually uncommon, collectively account for a substantial share of neurodevelopmental disorders, and each one offers a distinct and often underappreciated window into how the nervous system is built and maintained. These genes contribute to neural development and maturation at every stage of the process, from initial tissue patterning and progenitor proliferation through to the acquisition of mature cellular and circuit properties. Understanding how disruption of a single rare disease gene can cascade into complex developmental and cognitive phenotypes offers valuable insight into the biological basis of disorders such as autism, ADHD, and other neurocognitive symptoms that may arise due to altered gene function.

title: Integrative Psychiatry: Evidence, Mechanisms, and Clinical Application of Complementary and Lifestyle Approaches in Mental Health
summary: Mental disorders remain a major source of global disease burden, and despite substantial advances in contemporary psychiatry, many patients experience inadequate treatment response, adverse effects, or difficulties with long-term adherence to conventional interventions. Consequently, the use of complementary and integrative approaches to mental health care has grown considerably, driven by a perception of better tolerability and safety and patient preferences for holistic, person-centered, and culturally congruent models of care. At the same time, important concerns remain regarding the safety, efficacy, quality, and regulation of many complementary therapies, highlighting the need for rigorous scientific evaluation.

title: Advanced Molecular and Imaging Biomarkers for Neurological Disorders
summary: Neurological disorders are often driven by shared pathophysiological pathways, including immune dysregulation, glial activation, demyelination, and progressive neuronal loss. Imaging has become central to how these conditions are detected, staged, and monitored, with a comprehensive range of structural, functional, and molecular imaging modalities offering sensitive readouts of disease activity and progression. Yet the molecular meaning of many imaging signals is still only partly understood, which limits how far imaging can be used to reflect specific biological processes.

To tackle this limitation, we seek innovative unified frameworks that combine high-fidelity patient-specific soft tissue modeling, sim-to-real domain adaptation strategies, and closed-loop AI control guided by real-time medical imaging. title: Intergenerational Pathways to Mental Health
summary: Mental health problems often develop within a family and social context, and their effects may extend from one generation to another. Parental mental health problems, adverse childhood experiences, family violence, substance use, socioeconomic hardship, and disrupted family relationships can influence mental health outcomes in subsequent generations. At the same time, intergenerational transmission is not inevitable. Positive parenting, stable and supportive relationships, social support, access to mental health care, and other protective factors may reduce risk and contribute to better outcomes. Although interest in intergenerational mental health has grown considerably, important questions remain about how these influences interact at different stages of life and across different social and cultural settings. title: Neurobiological mediators of clinical outcomes in psychedelic-assisted therapies
summary: Psychedelic-assisted therapies have demonstrated rapid and often sustained clinical benefit across depression, PTSD, and other conditions. Neuroimaging, electrophysiological, and molecular studies increasingly link these effects to structural and functional neuroplasticity, supported by theoretical frameworks such as the Entropic Brain Hypothesis and REBUS. In parallel, clinical and qualitative research emphasizes the centrality of the subjective, phenomenological experience to therapeutic outcome. These two literatures — neurobiological and phenomenological — have largely developed in parallel, with few studies directly testing how they relate within the same patient sample. Consequently, whether neurobiological changes are causally responsible for clinical improvement, merely predictive of it, or simply co-occurring alongside a distinct psychological process remains an open and clinically consequential question.

title: Neuroinflammation and psychotic disorders: mechanisms, biomarkers, and treatment targets
summary: Neuropsychiatric research increasingly recognizes neuroinflammation as a critical mechanism underlying psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, and first-episode psychosis. Evidence from genetics, transcriptomics, neuroimaging, and peripheral immune profiling highlights the involvement of immune-related processes, particularly microglial activation, cytokine imbalance, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, and aberrant complement-mediated synaptic pruning, in shaping disease onset, cognitive impairment, and treatment resistance. These findings suggest that immune dysregulation is not merely a secondary phenomenon but a driving factor in illness progression. However, despite the surge of recent discoveries, the exact temporal dynamics, causal mechanisms, and the translational potential of immune signals remain incompletely understood. The integration of neurobiological, immunological, and clinical evidence offers a timely opportunity to bridge mechanistic insights

Many maintenance activities continue to expose workers to hazardous environments, repetitive tasks, confined spaces, and ergonomically challenging conditions. At the same time, industries are facing increasing pressure to improve productivity, reduce downtime, enhance safety, and address shortages of skilled maintenance personnel. summary: Headache disorders, such as migraine and cluster headache, are major contributors to global disability and often challenge both patients and clinicians with their persistence and complexity. Recent studies highlight that gaps remain between promising interventions tested in controlled settings and the outcomes realized in routine care, in part due to diagnostic uncertainties and real-world limitations. Ongoing debates involve how best to classify headache types, manage refractory cases, and ensure treatment safety over the long term. title: Spasticity and Pain in Neurological Disorders: Shared Pathways and Multimodal Rehabilitation Strategies
summary: The field of neurorehabilitation increasingly recognizes the entwined nature of spasticity and pain as disabling complications arising from neurological disorders. Traditionally considered and managed as distinct entities, spasticity and neuropathic pain are now understood to be underpinned by common mechanisms, including maladaptive central sensitization, spinal disinhibition, neuroinflammation, and altered supraspinal modulation. Their co-occurrence not only worsens functional impairment but also significantly degrades patient quality of life, making effective intervention an urgent need. Recent literature originating from multiple sclerosis research has introduced the concept of ‘Spasticity-Plus Syndrome’, which groups spasticity with spasms, pain, sleep disturbances, and autonomic dysfunction into an interconnected symptom cluster sharing common neurobiological substrates. title: Chronic stress, anhedonia, and reward-circuit dysfunction in depression: Mechanisms, models, and novel therapeutic approaches
summary: Chronic stress remains one of the most robust precipitants of major depressive disorder, in which anhedonia (the loss of motivation, pleasure, and interest) is a particularly disabling and treatment-resistant dimension. Converging evidence places the mesocorticolimbic reward system and connected hippocampal circuitry at the center of this pathology. Across the ventral tegmental area (VTA), nucleus accumbens (NAc), medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and hippocampus, sustained stress and allostatic load disrupt dopaminergic and glutamatergic signaling, functionally decoupling motivation, hedonic capacity, and reward learning.

ARFID is distinct from other eating disorders, as sensory sensitivities, fears surrounding adverse experiences with food, or lack of interest in eating, lead to considerable nutritional, physical, and psychosocial impacts rather than weight/shape concerns. Recent studies have highlighted complex neurobiological processes, atypical interoceptive awareness, and strong associations with neurodevelopmental and anxiety conditions underlying ARFID, yet its etiology, maintenance mechanisms, public health impact, treatment response, and presentation variation require further research exploration. title: Social Development and Mental Health: Policy Responses to Emerging Health Challenges
summary: Mental health is increasingly recognized as both a precondition and an outcome of social development. However, global advances have been uneven, reflecting deep structural inequalities in exposure to social risks and in the capacity of welfare systems to buffer their effects. A growing body of evidence shows that mental health outcomes are strongly shaped by social policies that regulate income security, employment conditions, education, housing, human mobility, and social protection across the life course. In many low- and middle-income countries, recurrent economic shocks, labor informality, weak social safety nets, and persistent uncertainty undermine psychological well-being at the population level. Despite the explicit inclusion of mental health within the Sustainable Development Goals, its integration into social and economic policy agendas remains limited, calling for more policy-relevant and context-sensitive research.

Persistent challenges in treating neurodegenerative diseases and neurological injuries stem from the limited capacity of the adult central nervous system for self-repair and regeneration. Recent research has illuminated pathways for overcoming these barriers, including reprogramming somatic cells into neuronal phenotypes and manipulating the epigenetic landscape to influence cell fate. Key breakthroughs demonstrate that targeted resetting of cellular identity can generate functionally relevant neurons, opening possibilities for reversing the effects of neurological disorders. summary: However, compared to structured environments such as industrial manufacturing and warehousing logistics, agricultural environments are far more complex and unpredictable. Scenarios such as farmlands, orchards, greenhouses, and hilly or mountainous areas typically present challenges including uneven terrain, severe crop obstruction, highly variable lighting conditions, unpredictable obstacle distribution, unstable communication conditions, and biological variability in the objects being handled. These factors significantly increase the difficulty of autonomous operation for agricultural robots and place higher demands on path planning, task scheduling, and intelligent decision-making methods. title: Motivational aspects of balancing eating and physical exercise in health and disease
summary: Food intake is an essential behavior for acquiring the energy required for survival. Because animals must expend energy through physical movement to obtain food, behavior is inherently constrained by the need to balance energy acquisition and expenditure. Maintaining this balance is fundamental for health. Traditionally, it has been framed from nutritional and metabolic perspectives. title: The Exercising Brain: Cognitive Neuroscience Perspectives on Physical Activity and Mental Health
summary: The relationship between physical activity and mental health has long been recognized; however, it has only been in recent decades that cognitive neuroscience has begun to elucidate the underlying neural mechanisms. Converging evidence from neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and neurochemical studies indicates that exercise induces profound changes in brain structure and function. These biological processes are increasingly understood to mediate the beneficial effects of physical activity on mood, cognitive function, and resilience to psychological stress. However, despite this progress, the cognitive neuroscience of exercise remains an underexplored frontier, with the precise mechanisms through which physical activity promotes mental health still incompletely understood.

title: Translating Desire – Psychology, Arts, and the Neuroscience of Pleasure
summary: Subjectively and phenomenologically, sexual arousal is a state of pleasure, joy, passion, and bodily excitement, followed by delight, positive exhaustion, and relaxation. Biologically, it involves changes in physiological arousal, the release of hormones and neurotransmitters in the autonomic nervous system and the central nervous system. In dimensional biological emotion theories, it represents the highly positive endpoint in the affective space defined by valence and physiological arousal, triggered by internal or external pleasurable and erotic stimuli. From an evolutionary perspective, the purpose of sexual arousal and pleasure is to prime action disposition for approach or avoidance, thereby supporting survival and driving perceptual, cognitive, and emotional resources through motivational systems that prioritize mating and influence decision-making about sexual behaviors.

title: Adverse Childhood Experiences and Addiction in Adolescence and Adulthood: from Research to Clinical Practice
summary: Traumatic experiences are recognized as a significant risk factor for the development of substance-related and behavioral addictions in both adolescence and adulthood. Despite extensive research, much work remains to be done to clarify the mechanisms underlying the relationship between trauma and the onset and maintenance of addictive behaviors. It is also necessary to understand the association between trauma and the emerging forms of behavioral or substance addiction observed in recent years. Further research should extend current knowledge to different cultural contexts and promote the development or adaptation of culturally sensitive tools for investigating the trauma–addiction relationship. Moreover, more scientific evidence is needed regarding the effectiveness of prevention and intervention programs, such as psychotherapeutic, social, or pharmacological interventions, for individuals with addictions who have been exposed to traumatic experiences.

title: Extracellular Vesicles in Ocular Physiology, Pharmacology, and Therapeutics
summary: Extracellular vesicle (EV) is a cell-released biological nanoparticle exploiting intrinsic mechanisms for molecular transport in the body. EVs are protected from extracellular degradation and can deliver RNA, DNA, protein, lipid cargo across the blood-brain and blood retinal barriers, making them an attractive carrier for biomolecules and drug delivery to the back of the eye. Recent research has suggested possible use of extracellular vesicles as biomarkers of various hereditary, metabolic and degenerative eye diseases. Currently, there are expected values to use them in the interpretation of disease severity level, progression and treatment responses, and to understand cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying a variety of ocular pathologies. Moreover, extracellular vesicles may open novel treatment options and drug delivery ways.

title: GPCR Receptor Complexes: Emerging Therapeutic Paradigms in Neuropsychiatry
summary: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) represent the largest pharmacologically exploited receptor superfamily in the human genome, accounting for the targets of approximately 35% of all approved drugs. In neuropsychiatry, GPCRs have long underpinned therapeutic strategies across a broad disease spectrum, from dopamine and serotonin receptor-based antipsychotics and antidepressants to opioid receptor-targeting therapies for addiction and pain. Despite this legacy, the conventional “one drug, one receptor” model has shown fundamental limitations: incomplete efficacy, dose-limiting side effects, high inter-individual variability, and persistent treatment resistance continue to burden clinical neuropsychiatric practice.

title: Health and Neuropsychological Determinants of Adaptation in Rare and Neurodevelopmental Disorders
summary: Rare and orphan diseases represent a major scientific and clinical challenge. Although each condition displays a low prevalence - affecting fewer than 5 in 10,000 individuals - collectively they impact an estimated 5–9% of the global population. Approximately 80% of these disorders are genetic in origin, with nearly three-quarters involving central nervous system impairment that frequently manifests as cognitive, behavioral, and emotional difficulties. Individuals with rare or orphan neurodevelopmental disorders, as well as their families and caregivers, face substantial psychosocial stressors related to diagnosis, uncertainty, treatment demands, and social stigmatization. Despite growing evidence on the neuropsychological mechanisms underlying these disorders, research integrating cognitive, emotional, and health-related factors remains limited. title: Neural Mechanisms of Human Movement, Cognition, and Emotion Across the Lifespan: Insights from Athletes, Older Adults, and Youth Using EEG and fNIRS
summary: The integration of motion capture and portable neuroimaging, specifically Electroencephalography (EEG) and functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS), has revolutionized movement science, allowing for the study of the brain in action. This advancement is crucial for understanding the intricate coupling between the brain, movement, cognition, and emotion. However, much research remains fragmented across different populations and life stages. We need to consolidate findings to understand how high performance is maintained in athletes, how mobility can be preserved in aging populations (e.g., gait and balance), and how physical activity supports healthy development in youth. A lifespan perspective using these ecological imaging tools is necessary to advance theory and practice.

Targeting Neuroinflammation in Spinal Cord Injury: From Inflammatory Mechanisms to Pharmacological Interventions
summary: Spinal cord injury (SCI) triggers a devastating secondary neuroinflammatory cascade—driven by microglial activation, immune infiltration, and sustained pro-inflammatory mediator release—that exacerbates tissue damage and impedes neurological recovery. The dynamic balance between pro-inflammatory (M1) and reparative (M2) phenotypes of microglia/macrophages has emerged as a critical determinant of injury outcome. Key signaling pathways, including NF-κB, NLRP3 inflammasome, TLR4, and the CCL2/CCR2 axis, represent promising pharmacological targets. Despite encouraging preclinical advances, effective clinical translation remains limited. This Research Topic aims to bridge mechanistic insights into SCI neuroinflammation with innovative pharmacological interventions, fostering the development of targeted therapies that can ultimately improve functional recovery after SCI.

The Interplay of Cognitive and Personality Variables in the Development of Ecological Identity and Healthy Behaviors
summary: Growing environmental threats and public health challenges have intensified interest in the psychological determinants of ecological awareness and sustainable living. While social and cultural influences have been widely studied, the role of cognitive functioning in shaping how individuals perceive, evaluate, and respond to environmental and health-related demands remains underexplored. Core cognitive processes, including executive functions, cognitive control, dual-process reasoning, episodic future thinking, attentional bias, and cognitive appraisal, are increasingly recognized as foundational to environmentally responsible decision-making and the adoption of healthy behavioral routines. Alongside these, personality dimensions such as empathy, emotional intelligence, and pro-environmental values operate as important modulators that shape the expression and efficiency of these cognitive mechanisms. title: Visually Guided Walking in Complex Environments: Neural, Biomechanical, and Translational Insights for Neuroprosthetics
summary: Walking is a deceptively complex behavior. Each step depends on the continuous integration of visual input, vestibular and proprioceptive signals, and motor commands distributed across cortical, subcortical, and spinal circuits. Vision plays a particularly central role: it anticipates obstacles, calibrates foot placement, and tunes locomotor control before the foot contacts the ground. When this visuomotor loop is disrupted by injury, neurological disease, aging, limb loss, or the use of a prosthetic or exoskeletal device, gait becomes slower, more variable, and metabolically costly. Mobile brain/body imaging (MoBI) including high-density EEG, fNIRS, EMG, inertial sensors, and motion capture, enables in-situ measurement of the brain and body during complex realistic behaviours. These advances have direct implications for neuroprosthetics: powered prostheses, exoskeletons, and brain–machine interfaces must ultimately operate inside the user’s own visuomotor control loop.

summary: High-throughput sequencing has democratized genomic research, enabling investigators to generate comprehensive 'omics datasets for virtually any species. Yet the development and curation of robust genomic and transcriptomic resources for non-traditional model organisms remains a significant challenge. Unlike established models such as Drosophila, C. elegans, or Mus musculus, many taxa with extraordinary biological traits, from cave-adapted species with convergent sensory evolution to marine invertebrates with remarkable neural plasticity, still lack well-annotated reference genomes, standardized transcriptomic atlases, or computational pipelines tailored to their biology. Bridging this gap is essential for unlocking comparative and evolutionary approaches to fundamental questions in genetics and neuroscience.

Traditionally, research on brain–organ interactions has been conducted in isolation, focusing on distinct axes such as the lung–brain, heart–brain, liver–brain, ovary–brain, gut–brain, kidney–brain, muscle–brain, and adipose–brain axes. However, mounting evidence reveals that these communication routes are deeply interdependent, with disruptions in one system capable of influencing neuroinflammation, cognition, behavior, and neurological disease progression. Conversely, changes in brain states and neural disorders can modulate the physiology and pathology of peripheral organs by altering autonomic balance, hormonal secretion, immune reactivity, circadian rhythms, and metabolic regulation. summary: The heart and brain are among the earliest and most metabolically demanding organs in human development. Though historically studied in isolation, both systems are developmentally and functionally intertwined, sharing vascular, inflammatory, metabolic, and genetic mechanisms. Disruption of these shared programs underlies a broad spectrum of cardiocerebral disorders, from congenital heart disease and stroke to Alzheimer’s disease, vascular dementia, and neurodevelopmental conditions.

Physiologically, external sonic pulsations can stimulate bodily response—innate vibrations within the body—to influence haemodynamic, neurological, and musculoskeletal functions. summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming perceptual science by offering novel ways to understand sensory perception and cognition. As computational power increases, so does our ability to model and simulate complex human perception processes. Self-organizing AI systems, particularly those utilizing machine learning algorithms like Self-Organizing Maps, have shown promise in mimicking complex perceptual phenomena. These advancements address fundamental questions about how neural mechanisms underlie sensory experiences and highlight ongoing debates concerning the limitations and capabilities of AI in replicating human-like sensory processing. Recent studies have highlighted the shortcomings of traditional diagnostic algorithms and have led to the development of new bedside examination techniques and imaging protocols. However, despite significant technological progress, deciphering the full mechanisms underlying how the brain generates cognition from dynamic neural activity remains a major scientific challenge. Key questions persist regarding how different scales of neural organization—from single neurons to large-scale brain networks—interact to support learning, memory, perception, and decision-making.

summary: Biomedical signal and image data analysis is a rapidly evolving field, focusing on the integration and interpretation of complex datasets sourced across various organs and scales. Recent advancements have highlighted the potential to analyze data across multiple spatial and temporal scales, using diverse modalities such as physiological signals like EEG, ECG, and EMG, along with imaging techniques including MRI, fMRI, CT, PET, and ultrasound. Although significant progress has been made, there remains a need to refine these methodologies to better encapsulate the multivariate nature of human physiology and its systemic interactions. This requires attention to the fusion of data from heterogeneous sources and addressing the multiorgan interactions to model comprehensive physiological and pathological processes.

The fusion of bionics’ structural emulation of biological entities, cybernetics’ feedback and control systems, and biorobotics’ application of these principles to achieve autonomous, adaptive locomotion forms the cornerstone of this research initiative. The aim is to advance the functional integration of these disciplines to create innovative robotic systems resembling biological locomotion and functionality.

title: Advances in Noninvasive Intracranial Pressure Monitoring Techniques
summary: Intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring is a critical aspect of managing patients with conditions such as traumatic brain injury, cerebral lesions, and intracranial hypertension. The gold standard for ICP monitoring involves invasive techniques, which are often unavailable in resource-limited settings. Noninvasive techniques, such as measuring the optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) with ultrasound or using transcranial Doppler techniques, have been extensively evaluated. However, concerns about bias, variations in ONSD thresholds, and inconsistencies in the literature have limited their routine use in clinical practice. Furthermore, no current noninvasive technology can fully replace invasive ICP monitoring, highlighting a significant gap in the field.

title: Advances in Understanding the Pathogenetic Mechanisms of Neurodevelopmental Disorders and Neurodegenerative Disease - The Environment as a Putative Risk Factor, Volume II
summary: Neurodevelopmental disorders and neurodegenerative diseases are conditions that arise from complex interactions between genetic and environmental factors, shaping brain development and function across the lifespan. The first volume of this Research Topic, Advances in Understanding the Pathogenetic Mechanisms of Neurodevelopmental Disorders and Neurodegenerative Disease - The Environment as a Putative Risk Factor , explored how genetic polymorphisms modulate the individual's susceptibility to environmental factors, such as neurotoxic metals and pesticides, that alter the trajectory of brain development. Evidence increasingly supports that conditions such as autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), Parkinson's disease (PD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) cannot be fully explained by genetic factors; instead, they emerge from a multifaceted interaction between a person's genetic background and their exposure to various environmental agents.

title: Brain Injury after Hypoxia/Ischemia: Mechanisms, Pathogenesis, and Potential Therapeutic Interventions
summary: Brain injury resulting from hypoxia (oxygen deprivation) or ischemia (restricted blood flow) represents a major challenge in medical research and clinical practice. Such injuries, often due to stroke, cardiac arrest, or asphyxiation, lead to significant consequences, including motor deficits, cognitive impairments, and increased mortality. The pathogenesis of these injuries involves a complex interplay of cellular and molecular events, including oxidative stress, inflammation, metabolic disruptions, excitotoxicity, and apoptosis. A deep understanding of these mechanisms is essential for developing effective therapeutic interventions. This research topic aims to thoroughly investigate the mechanisms driving hypoxia/ischemia-induced brain injury and identify novel therapeutic strategies to mitigate damage, promoting neuronal recovery and survival.

summary: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a significant public health concern, leading to considerable morbidity, mortality, and long-term disability across the globe. One of the major contributors to poor outcomes following TBI is cerebral edema, a secondary injury process characterized by excess accumulation of fluid in the brain parenchyma, which elevates intracranial pressure (ICP) and exacerbates neurological damage. Despite advances in the management of TBI, current therapies such as osmotherapy and decompressive craniectomy focus predominantly on controlling ICP rather than addressing the underlying mechanisms of edema. Emerging research highlights a crucial need to explore novel therapeutic strategies that directly target cerebral edema and its complex pathophysiology, as conventional approaches have not led to substantial improvements in patient outcomes.

Research efforts integrating human anatomy, functional neuroanatomy, and cellular neuroscience, including studies of vertebrate models, have been pivotal in revealing the intricate organization of basal ganglia circuits. In particular, dopaminergic neurons are crucial modulators within these networks, influencing processes ranging from nervous system development to the plasticity underlying learning and adaptation. Dysfunction of these circuits is implicated in various neurological and psychiatric conditions, emphasizing the importance of understanding their anatomy and physiology across different species and developmental stages.

title: Decoding Neurodegeneration: Insights into the Pathways of Neurological Decline
summary: Neurodegeneration is the gradual and progressive loss of neuron function and structure that ultimately leads to neuronal death. This phenomenon underlies a spectrum of debilitating disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, Huntington’s disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The hallmark of neurodegeneration is the aggregation of misfolded proteins, such as amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles in Alzheimer's or alpha-synuclein in Parkinson's, which disrupt cellular processes and trigger neuroinflammatory responses. Mitochondrial dysfunction is another critical factor, as impaired energy production and increased oxidative stress contribute to neuronal damage and apoptosis.

title: Design, Modeling, and Adaptive Control of Innovative Joints for Collaborative and Industrial Robotic Systems
summary: Robotic joints are indispensable components that directly determine the capabilities and performance of diverse robotic systems. In the domain of collaborative and assistive robots, adaptive joints are essential for enabling safe human-robot interaction, demanding compliance and adaptability to ever-changing environments. Current approaches employ soft actuators, variable stiffness mechanisms, and compliant transmission elements to enhance safety and operational efficiency. On the other hand, industrial robots necessitate joint designs that prioritize high precision, repeatability, and robustness. The intricate design of these joints balances compactness, reliability, and a broad spectrum of functional prerequisites, necessitating a multidisciplinary synthesis of expertise in mechanics, actuation systems, control algorithms, and materials science to deploy joints that not only function precisely but also adapt effectively to the specific demands of different robotic tasks.

title: Early Onset Schizophrenia and Cardiometabolic Risk
summary: Early onset schizophrenia (EOS) - defined as schizophrenia with onset before age 18 - presents with severe clinical symptoms, a chronic course, and significant functional impairment. Individuals diagnosed with EOS face a lifespan burden magnified by biological and environmental vulnerabilities, notably an increased risk of cardiometabolic comorbidities such as obesity, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. title: Embodiment in Cognition, Language, and Communication
summary: Embodiment in cognition, language, and communication examines how sensorimotor systems intertwine with language comprehension, suggesting that even the understanding of abstract expressions may be rooted in physical experience (Barsalou, 2010). The established body of research supports the idea that abstract cognition is not merely amodal or symbolic but is grounded in interactions between the body and environment (Aziz-Zadeh & Damasio, 2008; Gibbs, 2006; Johnson, 2015; Khatin-Zadeh et al., 2023). Cognitive neuroscience and psychology studies reveal that metaphorical language activates brain areas associated with perception and action, underscoring the impact of embodied experiences on conceptual structures (D’Angiulli, Griffiths, & Marmolejo-Ramos, 2015). Recognizing language's embodied nature is crucial; it is entwined with sensory, motor, and affective experiences, and structured through metaphorical mappings (Khatin-Zadeh & Vahdat, 2015).

summary: In recent decades biological imaging techniques have significantly improved, driven by the development of advanced optical, computational, and sample preparation techniques. title: Emerging Technologies and the Apparel Industry: Bridging Virtual and Physical Fashion Realms
summary: The digitization of the apparel industry is increasingly shaped by the integration of digital technologies and advances in computer science, making fashion a hybrid field that merges virtual and physical elements. Tools such as 3D body scanning and computer vision have introduced new levels of precision concerning sizing accuracy and consumer interactivity, offering remote customers vivid shopping experiences. VR and XR technologies are transforming consumer engagement and enriching fashion education by presenting immersive retail settings and digital classroom environments. Additionally, CAD and apparel simulation systems facilitate garment visualization and prototyping, improving communication between manufacturers and consumers, and reducing reliance on physical samples and material waste. Finally, the incorporation of data-driven approaches, digital twins, and human-computer interaction strategies expands further possibilities across design, supply chain management, and education.

Enhancing Brain Health: Physical, Cognitive, and Nutritional Interventions
summary: Brain health reflects the dynamic interplay of neural development, plasticity, and resilience across the lifespan. Emerging evidence shows that physical activity, cognitive engagement, and nutritional status each exert powerful, and often synergistic, effects on brain structure and function. These influences extend from early neurodevelopment through healthy ageing, and shape vulnerability to neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative conditions. At the same time, environmental exposures, genetic background, and lifestyle factors interact in complex ways that remain incompletely understood. Within clinical neuroscience, there is a growing need to clarify how targeted interventions in these domains can promote optimal nervous system development, preserve cognitive function, and mitigate disease risk. This Research Topic will integrate mechanistic, translational, and clinical research to delineate how physical, cognitive, and nutritional interventions can enhance brain health.

title: Enhancing mental health therapy with multi-omics and machine learning
summary: Mental disorders, affecting millions worldwide, present a significant challenge in clinical practice due to their complex etiology and varied manifestations. Traditional therapeutic approaches often fail to provide personalized care, underscoring the need for more innovative strategies. Multi-omics technologies, including genomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, allow for a broader understanding of biological processes. When these technologies are used in conjunction with advanced machine learning (ML) techniques such as generative AI and gradient boosting, there is potential to improve the specificity and effectiveness of treatments. This combination aims to better match therapies to individual patient profiles, potentially enhancing therapeutic outcomes and reducing adverse effects.

title: Enhancing robotic dexterity through advanced learning and multimodal perception
summary: Robotic manipulation is a dynamic field at the forefront of automation and artificial intelligence. Despite advances, challenges persist in ensuring robots can generalize across tasks, adapt to new environments, and collaborate with humans effectively. A notable limitation is the ability to perform contact-rich, fine-grained, and high-precision manipulation, crucial for real-world applications. Recent studies highlight a need for learning-based approaches, multimodal perception, and hierarchical planning strategies to overcome these barriers, aiming to improve dexterity and autonomous capabilities. Progressive efforts in the field have seen the rise of foundation models and visual-language-action models that integrate perception and action, allowing for nuanced manipulation tasks.

title: Enhancing safety and resilience in autonomous robotic systems: Addressing complexity with integrated AI and cybersecurity solutions.
summary: Autonomous robotic systems are increasingly evolving across diverse domains, including manufacturing, healthcare, autonomous vehicles, and space exploration. These systems' growth in autonomy and deployment in intricate and sometimes hazardous settings highlights the pressing need for their safety, security, robustness, and reliability. Historically, robotics heavily relied on deterministic control and pre-set behaviors, but the integration of machine learning, particularly deep learning, has ushered in more adaptable decision-making capabilities. Despite these advancements, new challenges emerge concerning unpredictability, explainability, and vulnerability to faults and cyber threats.

Recent breakthroughs in DNA methylation clocks, circulating biomarkers, and omics-driven profiling provide novel opportunities to unravel mechanisms of brain aging, improve early diagnosis, and enable targeted prevention strategies. Ergonomics of Recovery: Enhancing Mental or Cognitive Workload Relief and Well-Being in Contemporary Workplaces
summary: The field of workplace ergonomics has expanded rapidly in response to the cognitive, emotional, and physical demands of contemporary work environments, particularly as organizations adopt digital and hybrid modalities. In this context, mental workload—often used interchangeably with cognitive workload—refers to the psychological demands placed on attention, memory, and executive control during task performance. Advances in technology have increased flexibility and connectivity but also intensified risks of mental workload accumulation, psychological strain, and blurred work-life boundaries. Prolonged digital exposure, multitasking, and reduced restorative breaks can undermine employee well-being and performance. These challenges highlight the need to translate ergonomic and human factors principles into practical strategies that foster cognitive recovery, inclusivity, and sustainable organizational effectiveness.

title: Evidence of Off-Label Drug Use to Reduce Dementia
summary: Emerging evidence from basic, clinical, and epidemiological studies suggests that drug mechanisms of currently approved drugs can impact the risk and progression of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD). Repurposing existing drugs is a pathway for treatment that has worked for several other conditions (e.g., cancer, irritable bowel syndrome, erectile dysfunction) and this pathway to treatment can often be faster and more cost-effective than developing a new drug and going through the process to market approval. As ADRD grows as a public health problem placing a huge personal and financial cost on individuals, families, and the healthcare system, harnessing effective treatment quickly is key to reducing burden. Given the expense, safety risks, and substantial patient burden to receive treatment associated with lecanemab, the only current treatment available for AD, developing safe strategies for easier treatment is necessary.

title: Exploring Cognitive Deficits Across Various Sleep Disorders
summary: Sleep disorders, including but not limited to Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA), significantly affect cognitive function, impacting the quality of life and overall health. The interplay between sleep disturbances – such as excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) and sleep fragmentation - and cognitive deficits varies widely across different conditions. While much research has focused on OSA, other disorders like insomnia, narcolepsy, restless legs syndrome (RLS), shift work disorders, and circadian disruptions can exert similarly profound cognitive effects. Emerging studies have shed light on the diverse mechanisms through which these conditions impair neurocognitive functioning, emphasizing the roles of autonomic dysfunction and sleep fragmentation. However, a comprehensive understanding of the cognitive consequences across various sleep disorders remains incomplete, underscoring the need for a more in-depth exploration of their phenomenological and pathophysiological aspects.

Advances in molecular biology and genomics have catalyzed a paradigm shift from symptomatic treatment to mechanistic understanding, emphasizing the etiological role of genetic factors. Central to this shift is the emerging utility of genetic signatures—distinctive gene expression profiles that reflect underlying pathogenic processes. These signatures include coordinated transcriptional changes across gene networks, offering enhanced resolution over single-gene analyses. title: Homo Aquaticus: New Frontiers in Living and Working in the Ocean
summary: The ocean plays a critical role in the well-being of all humans on the planet, yet in many ways, we are still just at the beginning stages of ocean exploration. This gap in our understanding is particularly salient in the context of human presence within (as opposed to, on the surface of) the sea. Recent advances in several areas of marine research and technology as well as in the social sciences have the potential to re-envision how we work within the ocean, ranging from telepresence via robots to direct observation via brief visits using crewed submersibles to living on the seafloor using saturation diving. Yet the full potential of these methods to fully engage the non-scientific public requires a new paradigm for how Western societies live and work as part of the ocean, ideas envisaged using cutting-edge methods of storytelling such as film and serious games, and informed by multiple non-Western cultures.

title: Innovative electrode and bioelectronic technologies for neural recording and stimulation
summary: Neuroengineering is an ever-evolving field that is transforming our understanding of the nervous system through the development of sophisticated electrode and bioelectronic technologies. Traditional neural electrodes face significant challenges in interface stability, biocompatibility, long-term signal fidelity, and resolution, which hinder their broader application in neuroscience research and brain–machine interfacing. Recent studies have introduced innovations such as flexible materials, nano-scale architectures, and minimally invasive designs that promise higher integration with neural tissues, reduced immune response, and improved longevity. Despite these advances, achieving seamless, durable, and high-resolution communication with neural circuits remains one of the central challenges in next-generation neural interfacing.

title: Innovative experimental platforms in neuroscience research: from development to application
summary: Neuroscience research has recently experienced a dramatic evolution facilitated by the advent of sophisticated experimental platforms that imitate the human brain's structural and functional intricacies. Traditionally, monoculture systems prevailed, but now there's a shift towards dynamic, integrative models that can replicate the interactions between various cell types, their developmental paths, and environmental signals. Revolutionary approaches such as 3D cell cultures, brain organoids, and microfluidic devices have emerged as pivotal tools, offering translationally pertinent environments for understanding disease mechanisms, modeling brain development, and evaluating therapeutic interventions with improved consistency and predictive potency.

title: Integrating Avian Cognition: Bridging Interdisciplinary Gaps in Comparative Cognitive Science
summary: Avian behavior and cognition represent a fascinating field of study, offering insights into the evolutionary pathways that have shaped the cognitive abilities of birds. This has resulted in enhanced spatial learning and memory. Despite these differences, convergent evolution has led to shared traits between birds and mammals, such as long childhoods, extensive parental care, and warm-bloodedness, as well as complex social behaviors and cognitive abilities. summary: Neurological and mental health disorders represent a major challenge, impairing the quality of life for millions and exerting severe economic pressures, especially in under-resourced regions. The broad impact of these disorders spans beyond health deterioration to affect economic stability and development, prompting an urgent call for an integrated approach that melds neuroscience, innovative technology, and cohesive public health policies. Such disorders are particularly taxing in low- and middle-income countries, where healthcare systems struggle under the combined weight of inadequate resources and rising patient loads.

title: Interactions between the nervous, immune, and endocrine systems in brain health
summary: Brain health is the result of intricate communication between the nervous, immune, and endocrine systems. Traditionally, these systems were studied in isolation; however, recent advances highlight their dynamic crosstalk and their collective influence on brain function. Neuroinflammation, hormonal signaling, and immune responses are now recognized as critical factors in neurological development, homeostasis, and disease. Disruptions in these inter-system interactions are implicated in a myriad of conditions, such as neurodegenerative diseases, psychiatric disorders, and metabolic syndromes. As our understanding deepens, there is a growing appreciation for integrative approaches that examine these systems together, offering novel insights into mechanisms underlying brain health and disease.

title: Lipid Signaling in Neurological Disorders: From Neurodegeneration to Neuroinflammation
summary: The brain is composed of approximately 60% to 70% lipids, which primarily serve as structural components. However, many of these lipids also play critical roles in cellular signaling. In particular, sphingolipids and lysophospholipids function as second messengers, direct receptor ligands, and/or metabolic intermediates in various signaling pathways. Intracellularly, lysophospholipids serve as intermediate precursors for the biosynthesis of other lipids, whereas extracellular lysophospholipids act as signaling molecules that mediate diverse physiological processes. Dysregulation of sphingolipid and lysophospholipid metabolism has been increasingly associated with the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and multiple sclerosis, suggesting that lipid signaling plays a pivotal role in neuroinflammation, synaptic dysfunction, and neuronal survival.

The model specifies that cognition is dominated by perseverative negative thinking, commonly in the form of worry, rumination and fixated attention on threat. title: MicroRNA dysregulation and Apolipoprotein E in sporadic Alzheimer’s disease: molecular mechanisms, biomarkers, and sex-specific effects
summary: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) accounts for 60–80% of all dementia cases, with women at higher risk due to both longevity and biological factors. Familial AD, caused by mutations in APP, PSEN1, and PSEN2, represents less than 5% of cases, whereas sporadic AD (>90%) is mainly associated with polymorphisms in APOE and TREM2, which influence amyloid beta (Aβ) clearance. The APOE4 allele remains the strongest genetic risk factor for sporadic AD, yet the precise role of Apolipoprotein E (ApoE) in disease pathogenesis is still not fully understood.

Multidisciplinary perspectives on the processing of focus in human communication
summary: Focus, the grammatical means of highlighting information to convey meaning and intention, is a fundamental component of human communication, critical not only for oral interaction but also for advancing natural human-machine interfaces. Cross-linguistic research reveals profound diversity in how languages employ prosody, syntax, and semantics to mark focus, offering a window into language typology and evolution. At a neurocognitive level, focus processing is intimately linked to attention and prediction mechanisms, with neural correlates (e.g., activity in the superior temporal gyrus) being identified for intonational contours. Despite significant progress, an integrated understanding of focus across theoretical, experimental, and applied domains remains elusive.

title: Multimodal Perception and Biosignal Integration for Adaptive Healthcare Robotics
summary: Robotics is playing an increasingly vital role in healthcare, particularly through systems that monitor, assist, and respond to patient needs. A key enabler of this transformation is the integration of biosignals and multimodal perception—leveraging physiological data such as heart rate, EEG, EMG, and thermal imaging to adapt robot behavior in real time. These signals, when fused with visual, auditory, and contextual information, allow healthcare robots to provide personalized, safe, and effective interventions. However, challenges remain in standardizing biosignal interpretation, real-time data fusion, and ensuring robustness in clinical and home environments.

title: Multimodal Social Robots for Wellbeing and Health Support
summary: In recent years, social robots have moved from experimental visions to tangible implementations in education, healthcare, therapy, and everyday support. Their ability to sense and respond through multi-modal channels, including voice, movement, haptics, bio-signals, gestures and facial expressions, positions social robots as promising companions for well-being. This trend aligns with a growing societal interest in non-clinical health interventions and inclusive technologies that enhance resilience, autonomy, and improve quality of life. Social robots are increasingly being used to support interventions aimed at stress reduction, emotional regulation, and physical exercise. While progress has been made, further research is needed to understand how these multi-modal social robots for wellbeing and health support can be ethically designed, inclusively applied, and effectively evaluated across diverse contexts and populations.

title: Multimodal stimulation techniques
summary: Traditional neuromodulation techniques, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) or transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), have revolutionized our ability to non-invasively probe and alter brain activity. However, single-modality approaches often face inherent limitations in achieving highly specific or sustained effects due to the brain's distributed nature and compensatory mechanisms. A new frontier is emerging at the intersection of various stimulation methods and sensory inputs: multimodal stimulation. By combining distinct neurostimulation techniques (e.g., electrical, magnetic, optical, acoustic) with or across various sensory domains (e.g., visual, auditory, somatosensory), we can potentially unlock more sophisticated and targeted modulation of neural circuits, leading to enhanced understanding of brain function and more effective therapeutic interventions.

Feelings of connection to nature are related to increased sustainable behavior and environmental concern. However, the neuroscientific research in this continually growing field is still limited. Previous work to understand the neural correlates of environment processing, cognitive outcomes from environmental exposure, sustainable behavior, and environmental concern has employed both spectral and event-related EEG methodologies, as well as some neuro-imaging work. However, there is a need to study the human-environment psychological relationship from a neuroscientific perspective.

Contemporary views have broadened interoception to include not only visceral receptors but also their emotional and cognitive consequences. Interoceptive stimuli include mechanical, chemical, osmotic, glucose, and hormonal signals sensed by specialised receptors-mechanoreceptors, thermoreceptors, chemoreceptors, osmoreceptors, glucoreceptors, humoral receptors, and free nerve endings. title: Neurocognitive Shifts in Language Processing Across the Lifespan
summary: Language is not a fixed ability — it evolves with us. Behavioral, electrophysiological, eye-tracking, and neuroimaging studies have documented changes in comprehension, production, and lexical processing that reflect both neural adaptation and cognitive resilience. These shifts are shaped by the interplay between neurobiological maturation or decline, lifelong learning, and individual patterns of engagement with language-rich environments.

Neurogenic Shoulder Abduction Disorder
summary: Neurogenic shoulder abduction disorder is caused by trauma- or non-trauma-induced damage to the C5 nerve root or its branches, resulting in denervation of the muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and deltoid). It is a common shoulder joint disease that seriously affects patients' daily lives and work abilities. The etiology of non-traumatic C5 nerve root lesions causing shoulder abduction disorder is complex, such as neuritis, nerve root diseases, etc. Currently, drug therapy - including vitamin B1, B6, mecobalamin, and coenzyme Q10 - is mainly used. However, the therapeutic effect is limited. For traumatic C5 nerve root injuries, surgical repair is primarily employed at present, such as accessory nerve transfer to the suprascapular nerve, triceps branch of the radial nerve transfer to the axillary nerve, or intercostal nerve transfer to the axillary nerve, etc.

title: Neuroimaging for early detection and intervention in Alzheimer’s and cognitive disorders
summary: Neuroimaging has revolutionized our understanding of Alzheimer's disease and cognitive disorders. These advanced techniques bridge the gap between microscopic brain changes and clinical symptoms. Once focused on large anatomical changes, today's technologies include high-resolution tractography and molecular PET imaging, which visualize white matter connectivity and track proteins like amyloid and tau. By integrating structural, functional, and molecular insights, these tools deepen our understanding of cognitive decline. However, critical gaps remain, necessitating new strategies for optimal integration and application. Protocol harmonization, early detection in preclinical stages, and differentiating Alzheimer's from related dementias are urgent challenges.

Neurovascular Inflammation in Aneurysm Pathogenesis and Its Contribution to Neurodegenerative Processes
summary: Neurovascular inflammation represents a critical area of research in understanding the dynamics of aneurysm formation and rupture, known precursors to subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) and subsequent cerebral vasospasm. These events can lead to secondary neuronal injury, highlighting an important connection to neurodegenerative processes. Pathological neuroinflammation has emerged as a primary driver in these mechanisms, where initial endothelial damage - precipitated by factors like hypertension, genetic predispositions, or lifestyle choices such as smoking - initiates maladaptive vascular inflammation. This cascade involves monocyte infiltration and cytokine release, notably IL-6, which compromises vessel integrity and encourages aneurysmal expansion and rupture.

title: New Perspectives on the Role of Sensory Feedback in Speech Production: Volume IV
summary: Speaking represents one of our most complex motor behaviors, one that is vital to our ability to communicate. To understand how speech is produced, one crucially important question to address is: how is sensory feedback used in the speech production process? Answering this question is an important step to understanding how the motor skill of speaking is initially learned and then maintained, as numerous studies have shown that sensory feedback plays a key role in these learning processes. There is also evidence that sensory feedback is important for successful moment-by-moment control of ongoing speech output. It is natural, therefore, that significant portions of current models of speech production are devoted to explaining the role of sensory feedback. Furthermore, abnormal processing of sensory feedback appears to be involved in many disorders of speech and voice production, like laryngeal dystonia and stuttering.

Post-stroke Epilepsy: Risks, Prognosis, and Prevention
summary: Poststroke epilepsy (PSE) is one of the most common complications of stroke, affecting approximately 10% of patients. Stroke is also the most common cause of epilepsy in older people. PSE must be carefully differentiated from early epileptic seizures, which occur in the first seven days after stroke onset. PSE can develop in patients due to the structural brain damage caused by the stroke, leading to abnormal electrical activity that results in seizures. It has been linked to poor functional outcomes, neurocognitive deficits, and higher mortality. Additionally, people with PSE can experience an overall decline in quality of life owing to factors such as reduced employability and driving restrictions. Therefore, identifying factors that might increase an individual’s likelihood of developing PSE, coupled with timely and appropriate therapeutic interventions, is essential to optimizing management of those with this disorder.

title: Realistic multi-scale modeling of neural circuit dynamics - Volume II
summary: We are pleased to announce this Volume II Research Topic, building upon the impactful contributions and insightful discussions generated by the first Research Topic in this series - 'Realistic Multi-Scale Modeling of Neural Circuit Dynamics'. Neural circuit dynamics remain profoundly complex, underpinned by intricate interactions spanning molecular, cellular, and network scales. While significant advancements in computational neuroscience have enabled the development of increasingly detailed biophysical models, the fundamental challenge persists: effectively bridging these disparate scales to achieve truly comprehensive and predictive simulations. This ongoing endeavor is crucial for advancing our understanding of brain function and dysfunction, necessitating continued exploration and innovation in multi-scale modeling approaches.

title: Recent Advances in the Stabilization and Integration of Associative Memories
summary: The potential to adapt our behavior in response to environmental demands relies on our ability to generate and update memories of relevant information. After learning, memories undergo consolidation, a process that strengthens memory traces and transforms them into stable, long-lasting forms. On a cellular level, learning triggers rapid posttranslational modifications, such as the synthesis of plasticity-related proteins, facilitating synapse formation and maturation. On the circuit level, various brain areas form networks crucial for learning and memory. The most studied is the one involving the hippocampus, neocortex, and limbic nuclei, which are essential for memory consolidation. According to system consolidation theory, memories are initially encoded by the hippocampus and later transferred to the neocortex. This idea has been backed by studies that reveal coordination between hippocampal reactivations and cortical oscillations during sleep.

summary: The rising prevalence of mental health disorders has made them a major public health challenge. These conditions exhibit complex pathological mechanisms and high individual heterogeneity. Conventional research methods are limited in mechanistic depth and diagnostic objectivity, impeding precision medicine. Artificial intelligence (AI), including large language models, offers new pathways for investigating disease mechanisms and building diagnostic or predictive models by leveraging its strengths in data mining and pattern recognition. However, the "black-box" nature of AI leads to insufficient interpretability, which severely restricts its clinical translation. There is an urgent need for systematic research on AI-assisted disease mechanism interpretation, optimization of model explainability, and precision modeling. title: Resource‑ and Energy‑Aware Multi‑Robot Operations: Scheduling, Recharging, and Long‑Horizon Persistence
summary: Battery capacity, recharge logistics, and computational budgets are now the primary bottlenecks for scaling multi robot systems from short demos to dependable, 24/7 operations. Long horizon missions—warehousing, inspection, agriculture, environmental monitoring, and public safety—require fleets to coordinate tasks, routes, and recharge events while accounting for battery aging, stochastic demand, uncertain travel times, and heterogeneous platforms. Classical planning or perception advances alone are insufficient: persistence hinges on resource models, predictive energy usage, and infrastructure aware scheduling that closes the loop between algorithms, chargers, and the physical environment. This Research Topic focuses on the algorithmic and systems foundations that make multi robot autonomy sustainable and economically viable over days to months, emphasizing measurable mission availability, throughput, safety under energy constraints, and total cost of ownership.

title: Rewiring Recovery: The Role of Cognitive-Motor Integration in Neurorehabilitation
summary: In rehabilitation medicine, the integration of cognitive and motor functions is essential, especially in neurological and neurodegenerative disorders where central nervous system damage affects both domains. Cognitive-Motor Syndrome (CMS) and Motoric Cognitive Risk (MCR) syndrome highlight this dual impairment, linking disruptions in cognition, movement, and sensory systems. These conditions are associated with structural brain changes, inflammation, and neurotransmitter imbalances, requiring multidisciplinary assessment and intervention.
